POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:32:33 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals https://www.politico.eu/article/the-winners-and-losers-of-the-eu-uk-summit-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:24:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9366021 BRUSSELS — U.K. and EU leaders on Friday hailed a “win-win” as they announced long-awaited deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The reality is more complicated.

A summit press conference failed to resolve questions over whether the much-lauded food and drink rules, emissions trading and youth visas deals are contingent on a tuition fees agreement set to be negotiated over the next six months.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that the deals are “done” and tuition fees are still to be negotiated — despite EU claims to the contrary earlier on Friday.

If all the agreements take effect, there will be winners and losers on both sides of the English Channel and beyond. We take stock of who’s up and who’s down.

Winners

Students 

British and EU students are among the biggest winners from today’s announcements, benefiting from both a youth experience scheme and the planned tuition fee deal.

Under the new scheme, 100,000 young people will be able to spend up to three years working or studying in Britain or the EU respectively — a significant improvement on current visa requirements.

Under a deal yet to be thrashed out, students could also benefit from lower tuition fees when studying abroad. Two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, said London had so far offered fees of £12,000. The EU would drop its fees too.

If agreed, this would be a significant win for Brussels, with EU students currently subject to international student rates of up to £38,000 per year in the U.K.

British supermarkets

U.K. supermarkets — many of whom import from and export to the EU — were among the first to praise the agrifood deal, with major brands like Tesco and M&S saying the deal would make it easier and cheaper to trade with Europe.

The deal will see Britain align with EU food and agriculture rules by 2028, removing the need for costly certification requirements and checks in a move the U.K. government claims could add up to £5.1 billion a year to the British economy. 

“Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said M&S managing director Alex Freudmann. “When this deal comes into force, it will remove this bureaucracy.”

That said, there are questions over whether retailers will be in a position to pass on any savings to the customer amid spiraling energy costs.

Renewables providers

British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers. 

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,”  RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.”  EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry

The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.

The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.

The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.

Of the more political parts of the agreement, the Youth Experience Scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

The City has been shut out of EU markets since Brexit, with only London’s clearinghouses, a key part of the plumbing of the financial system, maintaining the ability to directly serve European clients. Brussels for years refused to even talk to Britain about financial services until issues on the Northern Ireland border were resolved.

Now, as Burnham pushes for better, financial services could yet benefit. While the City is in no great rush to give up the new U.K. regulatory regime developed since Brexit, there is hope of more collaboration in areas like investment, particularly for defense and start-ups, where both sides face a lack of cash and fears over economic resilience

Losers

British universities

With so much potentially hinging on a tuition fee deal, the U.K. government is under increasing pressure to get this agreement over the line. 

But it’s also under a lot of domestic pressure from universities, which have warned the move could cost them £500 million a year — money that they say would otherwise be used to help fund research, teaching and jobs.

Currently, tuition fees for EU nationals studying in the U.K. can reach up to £38,000 per year, in line with other international students, while British students pay a maximum of £9,790 a year in England.

Hollie Chandler, director of strategic policy at the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said any reduction in EU student fees would “put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.”

Chinese carmakers

It could have been worse for Chinese carmakers, but they aren’t in the clear just yet.

The EU wanted the U.K. to agree to a commitment binding it to the EU’s tariff regime on Chinese cars and other imports. The U.K. successfully pushed back, instead saying it would “ensure outcomes consistent with the relevant EU measures in order to ensure that the supply chain in question is protected in a consistent way” across the two markets and “guard against potential risks of circumvention.”

But as talks over British access to the EU’s Made in Europe industrial scheme continue over the coming months, that phrasing leaves the door open to raising tariffs in the future.

China experts Gregor Williams and Noah Barkin had previously warned that “acting before the terms of Made in Europe access are settled would weaken London’s negotiating leverage.”

“The UK has an incentive to signal a willingness to align with the EU while stopping short of imposing immediate restrictions on Chinese imports, not least given Beijing’s threats of retaliation,” Williams and Barkin added. They expect “some form of UK trade action on Chinese vehicles will come in the next 12 months.”

Food manufacturers

A major selling point of the SPS deal is the idea that it will bring down food prices for British consumers — one that government ministers have pounced on during the cost-of-living crisis fueled by the Iran war. 

But U.K. food firms have taken issue with this framing, pointing out that alignment with EU rules will mean costly changes for manufacturers as they align with EU requirements on issues like food safety, packaging, labeling and pesticides.

In guidance published alongside the summit statement, the U.K. government sets out a series of transitional arrangements aimed at helping firms adapt to the new changes.

While she welcomed the prospect of closer trade ties with the EU in the longterm, Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, warned that “the timing remains tight.” She urged the U.K. government to pass the relevant legislation and publish detailed business guidance “as quickly as possible” to give firms time to make necessary changes.

British steelmakers

The deal might be a win for steelmakers in the long-run, but the sector will have to wait some time to feel the benefits.

While the emissions trading scheme deal will ultimately spare Britain’s steel producers from the EU’s carbon border tax regime, it won’t take effect until 2028, leaving British producers exposed for at least another year.

Brussels and London are also still in talks to forge a steel alliance that would see the two sides harmonize new quota and tariff regimes imposed in July after they slashed market access for each other. But they couldn’t get things wrapped up in time for the summit and talks are proving challenging.

Defense firms

Although the two sides committed to immediately setting up a new Dialogue on Economic Security to tackle shared economic dependencies, they said little about defense sector collaboration.

Reviving talks for Britain to get access to the EU’s €150 billion SAFE fund for joint defense procurement loans “isn’t part of the summit negotiation,” Britain’s Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said Friday. But if the EU “wanted to return to it, I’d certainly suggest we’d be willing to do so,” he told Sky News.

Potentially significant language in the joint statement includes plans to “enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues,” including the prospect of British involvement in the EU’s “Capability Coalitions” — groups of member states which pool resources and coordinate investment in making new defense capabilities.

]]> en Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-eu-uk-summit-reset-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9365667 BRUSSELS — Hours before Andy Burnham arrived at a long-planned U.K.-EU summit Friday, it seemed like it’d be a humdrum victory lap.

Talks ran late Thursday but that always happens; Britain seemed to believe everything was wrapping up as planned; Burnham even brought a super-delegation of seven Cabinet colleagues. “Deal done,” texted one U.K. official at 14 minutes to midnight.

The spin war only came Friday morning — and not for the first time in Britain’s long Brexit saga, it arrived in a dry technical briefing in the European Council’s Europa building HQ.

A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling.

Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa.

They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what. 

Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.”

“The U.K. wanted to get something on Made in Europe, so that meant tuition fees being delayed as well. Somehow this has turned into a great defeat for the U.K. government because everything would be at the mercy of tuition fees,” he said. “That was what the U.K. government actually wanted.”

Opposition politicians seized on the row, with Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage calling Burnham “naive.” Oliver Lewis, the former Conservative Brexit aide who has founded a new anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, said he had “been played like a fiddle by Brussels.”

Brussels waffle

If intended to seize the narrative, the statement worked. 

Other EU officials tried to downplay its significance as the morning unfolded — the key phrase “equal treatment” was, in fact, not in the final summit text — but the issue still dominated questions at a joint press conference by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

U.K. officials sprang up an unplanned briefing to counter-spin while Downing Street aides texted journalists with lines from a government spokesperson saying the deal was done. Burnham himself told the press conference: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done. It’s there in black and white.”

A senior U.K. official insisted to POLITICO that the three deals on food standards, emissions and youth experience were not contingent on a pact on tuition fees.

Yet EU diplomats continued to suggest they were part of a “package,” a concept neither Costa nor von der Leyen tried very hard to shoot down. (Von der Leyen told journalists merely that the tuition fees deal was “on a different sheet of paper,” before Burnham was treated to a battered fish lunch with a dessert of fruit with actual Brussels waffle.)

Later Friday, Britain’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO he was “confident” that a tuition fees deal would be reached over the next six months.

But the risk is not negligible. The six-month deadline to ink an agreement includes a French presidential election; if the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins it could have unpredictable results for the EU’s legislative agenda, including Made in Europe. And negotiations on the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (the legislation behind Made in Europe) are behind schedule, with talks between the Council and European Parliament yet to begin and disagreements over the automotive package adding to the complexity.

Lower tuition fees, please

The Commission and Council statement Friday morning seized the headlines for two reasons.

The first was that it indicated the three deals tied up on Thursday night would not go ahead if Britain broke its promise to cut tuition fees. EU officials insisted they were not holding Britain “hostage,” but it was difficult to interpret the statement otherwise.

The second was the phrase “equal treatment” — which appeared to suggest the whole deal was contingent on something Britain was not even willing to offer.

Britain has signaled it will cut the international fees charged by U.K. universities — often well over £30,000 per year — to a lower level for students coming from the EU. 

But crucially, the U.K. has resisted European demands to match EU students’ fees with the £9,790-a-year “home fees” paid by U.K. students. Instead both sides have talked about a figure somewhere in the middle; negotiators have discussed a possible figure of £12,000 in private, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, who like others cited in this story were granted anonymity to share candid details.

This is a deeply personal issue for many European politicians and diplomats, who either spent their youths at Britain’s famed elite universities — think Oxford, Cambridge or the London School of Economics — or now have children attending them, or hoping to, at least.

There were immediate suspicions on the U.K. side that the EU’s statement was a piece of spin in the midst of a negotiation.

The U.K. is holding its cards close on tuition fees to keep leverage over Made in Europe. A resolution on both issues was delayed because Made in Europe, designed to protect the bloc’s industries from a flood of cheap imports, remains in its early stages. The summit text agreed by the U.K. and EU contained no direct reference to the scheme, merely a pledge to “limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains.”

Despite this, there was a view in the British contingent that the U.K. pushed the EU successfully for assurances on Made in Europe — meaning the EU had to flex its muscles somewhere else.

“It was a pretty complicated discussion, and the British took a very hard line,” said one EU diplomat. This person added: “The discussion on tuition fees fell out because of the issue related to equal treatment… Ultimately, it’s not the statement we would have wanted, but with a partner like this, it’s important to maintain dialogue.”

‘Dear Andy’

Both sides put on smiles at the press conference, with Burnham calling the deals a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe.” Von der Leyen heaped praise on the man she referred to from the podium as “dear Andy.”

Ultimately, the most important question about Friday’s row will be whether the deals Burnham announced are at any genuine risk of falling apart. 

“Six months seems a bit short to me” to sort out the tuition fees issue, said the EU diplomat quoted earlier in this story. British officials insist there is no issue.

To make matters more complicated, Brussels is also pressing London to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, potentially tying this to Made in Europe provisions. The U.K. has yet to decide, though there is a widespread expectation among Labour MPs and some ministers that Britain will end up raising tariffs on Chinese EVs.

If Friday’s deals do go ahead, the spin battle will be filed alongside countless other technocratic spats of the Brexit wars that fade into background noise.

But even so, the deals are not expected to see the light of day until at least 2028 — undercutting Burnham’s pitch to the British public that they will cut food costs and ease business red tape. (The prime minister highlighted Treasury analysis that showed Friday’s deals could add 0.5% or £17 billion to U.K. GDP.)

Implementation of the agrifood deal is not planned until March 2028, while a deal to link the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems is only expected in the same year — meaning British firms will see no immediate relief from EU carbon border taxes, a further blow to the struggling steel industry.

With the youth experience scheme not expected to be up and running until 2030, there are also questions over whether the program will survive the next election, which must happen before August 2029.

There will be other challenges in selling the deal too. The U.K. claimed a late breakthrough on Thursday night in securing a role in shaping EU food standards rules — but hours later, Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds suggested Britain’s role would be limited. “We’d have experts in the room. We’d have the ability to put our point of view into that process. We’re not getting a vote because we’re not a member of the EU,” Reynolds told the BBC.

Farage seized on this Friday, saying Britain would be forced to follow European rules on agricultural technology and pesticides rather than forging its own path.

‘Informal brainstorm’

Perhaps most importantly, Friday’s spin war is a reminder that nothing in Brussels is ever easy. It is a collision between Burnham’s big-picture way of doing politics and the EU’s hard, rules-based world.

This will matter for a prime minister who plans to stake much of his campaign at the next election on a battle for hearts and minds over Europe. That ballot isn’t due until July 2029, but Farage predicted on Friday that the election would come as soon as May 2027, about a year after Burnham’s ascent from the Greater Manchester mayoralty to Westminster.

As POLITICO reported this week, the personally pro-rejoin Burnham has not decided exactly what to promise the British public — and is caught between his aspirational rhetoric and the reality of a divided Cabinet. Now he can throw in the difficulty of dealing with the EU too.

Costa reflected this neatly in the press conference, telling Burnham he was “always welcome in the EU” — but almost in the next breath, reminding him that the EU’s principles, including the “indivisibility” of free movement from access to the single market, would “guide our engagement with the United Kingdom.”

Burnham plans to set out the options he believes are available for the future relationship next month, tied in with his promised “10-year plan” for Britain. It will kick-start a conversation that will likely culminate in a Europe-shaped offer to the public in Labour’s election manifesto.

But he also indicated Friday that he would not seek more policy-by-policy deals with the EU ahead of the next election, instead favoring a broader conversation. Even Starmer promised “iterative” deals once per year.

The U.K. prime minister also continued to be vague about how that process would unfold. He spoke of “informal brainstorming” with the EU ahead of another summit next year. “We are open for brainstorming,” Von der Leyen replied.

Sebastian Starcevic, Sam Francis and Sam Blewett contributed reporting.

]]> en France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership https://www.politico.eu/article/france-germany-complete-political-deal-for-ecb-leadership/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:50:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9348045 FRANKFURT — France and Germany on Friday submitted their candidates to fill two looming vacancies on the European Central Bank’s Executive Board, completing a political package that’ll decide the institution’s leadership for years to come.

Berlin presented Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, as the ECB’s next chief economist, after the Irish incumbent Philip Lane concludes his eight-year term on May 31.

Paris put forward Laurence Boone — a former minister of Europe and political ally of President Emmanuel Macron — who is now head of corporate and investment banking at Santander, to take over the ECB’s markets portfolio. That post will become available on Jan. 4, when Isabel Schnabel leaves the ECB for a job at the International Monetary Fund.

The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7.

The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said.

If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year.

In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets.

“I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.”

Fewer politicians

A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency.

De Cos and Vice-President Boris Vujčić are seasoned central bankers, as is Piero Cipollone, who heads the payments department. Before becoming a politician, Boone had been chief economist at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

While the reshuffle will leave the six-strong board looking more apolitical, the game of ECB musical chairs has been anything but, according to ING’s head of macro, Carsten Brzeski.

“It looks like another masterpiece of French diplomacy and strategic personnel policy,” he said. “With the move to opt for the markets operation, France gave the impression of passing the more important job of chief economist to Germany.”

“However, with a Spanish president and France holding the markets operation, the risk of a more dovish ECB has clearly increased,” Brzeski said.

“So far, I only know the proposals from media reports,” he said, adding that such options should not be discussed publicly but “with Ukraine and all other parties involved, including the Europeans.”

“You cannot negotiate this over other people’s heads,” Pistorius said. “Every idea deserves to be examined, but not every idea is equally good. As for this particular one, I don’t know which applies,” he added. “We will have to see in the upcoming talks.”

]]> en Marine Le Pen’s party faces scrutiny over alleged leaks from interior ministry https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-le-pen-national-rally-party-alleged-interior-ministry-leaks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:56:27 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9363414 PARIS — French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Friday summoned a senior civil servant who is under judicial investigation for allegedly leaking confidential information to the far-right National Rally.

Hugues Moutouh, the senior state representative in the Centre-Val de Loire region, is under investigation by prosecutors in Paris for reportedly passing on information about judicial investigations into Marine Le Pen’s party, according to multiple French outlets including Le Monde, which first reported on the allegations.

The investigation was opened in July and Moutouh has not been formally charged, Le Monde reported. Civil servants are bound by professional confidentiality, and sharing information on a judicial investigation is also an offense under French law.

On Friday, Nuñez confirmed that Moutouh was being investigated but said he was not informed of the details of the inquiry. “If the allegations are verified, they are obviously very serious,” Nuñez told BFMTV. The interior minister also said he would see Moutouh on Friday morning.

Moutouh could not be directly reached for comment. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Police reportedly carried out raids at the headquarters of the National Rally and at the interior ministry, Le Monde reported. Investigators looking into allegations of misuse of EU funds found documents which raised suspicions that the National Rally had received confidential judicial information.

“The National Rally will not comment this ongoing investigation and stresses the confidentiality of judicial inquiries,” Bruno Bilde, a National Rally official, said in a statement.

]]> en Some oil giants to be labeled green under EU finance rules https://www.politico.eu/article/some-oil-giants-will-now-be-labeled-sustainable-under-eu-finance-rules/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:38:49 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9362742 BRUSSELS — Some of the world’s biggest oil companies will be able to promote themselves as green investments in the EU under an overhaul of the bloc’s sustainable finance rules.

EU member countries and lawmakers struck a deal late Thursday to update the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation that will make it easier for private investment earmarked for green activities to flow into new fossil fuel projects.

It was Big Oil’s second big European win of the day, after the EU agreed early Thursday to delay methane emission rules for fossil fuel companies for two years.

The sustainable finance agreement substantially loosens a proposal by the European Commission to get more money flowing into companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models.

The executive decided to overhaul the SFDR, which aims to prevent greenwashing and help investors make sustainable investment decisions, last November. It proposed introducing three new categories for green funds — ESG basics, Transition and Sustainable — which each have progressively stricter sustainability criteria.

EU countries and the European Parliament had disagreed over whether fossil fuel companies should be allowed in the new “transition” category. The Commission proposed a blanket exclusion, but member countries pushed for oil companies with greener ambitions to be included.

The Parliament, meanwhile, only wanted oil and gas companies to be allowed if they invest more in green activities than in new oil and gas projects over a three-year period.

Under Thursday’s final agreement, seen by POLITICO, the EU has ruled that companies will have to spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities and this will have to “meaningfully” increase “over time” and be measured annually.

The increase in green investment cannot be “merely marginal or nominal,” the rules specified. The 20% capex threshold will be reviewed by the Commission in five years.

Companies will also have to produce a Paris-aligned emissions reduction plan for some of their emissions. However, downstream emissions — which represent the biggest share of oil and gas companies’ emissions — will not have to be covered by these plans.

The EU’s finance chief, Maria Luís Albuquerque, told POLITICO that the final deal was “close enough” to the Commission’s proposal as she left the meeting.

The outcome could see big oil and gas companies like France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol qualify for financing under the transition category, based on their 2025 capital expenditure.

The French oil giant met with the lead Parliament negotiator, Dutch MEP Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, three times between the start of 2025 and June 2026, according to Parliament documents.

Aleksandra Palinska, executive director at sustainable finance trade association Eurosif, said the criteria agreed by the co-legislators on the transition category “fail to distinguish companies genuinely transforming their business models from those making isolated green investments.”

Capitals win

EU capitals proposed a more lenient approach than the Commission and Parliament, agreeing in June that Big Oil could be included in the transition category if companies spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities, as defined under the EU taxonomy on sustainable investments.

This is despite several EU countries advocating for a move away from fossil fuels and publishing fossil fuel phase-out plans at COP31 this month.

Lawmakers in October voted for big oil and gas companies to only be included in the category if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period.

Several EU countries — including France and Italy — saw the Parliament’s position as a “red line,” according to a document seen by POLITICO, with the final agreement landing closer to what EU capitals wanted.

Despite this, Gerbrandy, who led negotiations in Parliament, said he was happy with the agreement. “I think we achieved a result that is in accordance with the criteria I set — credibility and administrative burdens — so I’m very satisfied,” he said.

]]> en ‘Staff deserve answers’ on Commission cyberattack, union says https://www.politico.eu/article/staff-deserve-answers-eu-commission-cyberattack-union-says/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:04:39 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9363012 BRUSSELS — A European Commission staff union has hit out at the EU executive for keeping officials in the dark after they first heard about a major cyberattack against the EU institution when it was reported by POLITICO.

A cyberattack against the Commission potentially compromised swaths of personal data at the EU executive and left staff unable to input salary and leave information, POLITICO first reported on Thursday.

The Commission has since publicly acknowledged the incident but it is “yet to send a single update to all staff, let alone provide a comprehensive explanation of the incident,” Cristiano Sebastiani, chair of the European Commission branch of the Renouveau & Démocratie (R&D) union, wrote in an email seen by POLITICO.

The lack of internal communication is “unacceptable,” he wrote in the email, titled “Staff deserve answers now.”

“It’s simply inconceivable that news outlets around the world are covering the incident while staff are still waiting for their first direct update from the Commission,” he wrote, adding that current and retired colleagues have written to R&D with concerns.

The union has several thousand members, Sebastiani said in a comment.

Some staff told R&D that managers denied a cyberattack had taken place and said the incident was a routine technical issue, Sebastiani wrote in the email.

The lack of communication is especially grave because internal HR systems are affected, meaning sensitive personal data may be at risk, the union representative wrote. He called for the Commission to immediately explain the incident to all staff, including information about what data was affected, and to carry out an independent review.

The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor, the internal EU data watchdog, a spokesperson for the regulator said.

The Commission did not immediately respond to a request about the union email. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Thursday that the Commission took “the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” adding that individual systems were targeted and that “in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:45:05 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 Russian missiles over Poland, European troops in the mud: Ukraine’s defence force is taking shape https://euobserver.com/250435/russian-missiles-over-poland-european-troops-in-the-mud-ukraines-defence-force-is-taking-shape/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:33:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250435 Just hours before the European war games in Poland began, Russian missiles and a drone tore through its Nato airspace.]]> The air raid sirens came at around 6.30AM on Friday (20 November) near Nowa Dęba, a small town in south-east Poland, roughly 100km from the border with Ukraine.

At least two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone had violated Polish airspace during the morning even as troops from 11 European countries had gathered in a large field surrounded by tall pine tree forests nearby.

The Russian cruise missiles and drone hit areas in south-eastern Poland, one 50km from Ukraine’s border. Nobody was killed.

“Common sense suggests there are no coincidences in such incidents. I think it was some kind of incident linked to our presence here,” Dariusz Mendrala, a major general in the Polish Armed Forces and the chief of the Armed Forces Support Inspectorate, told reporters.

“It won’t stop us from preparing to carry out our mission. For us, for the Polish state, for the Polish Armed Forces, these things have not been entirely exceptional for some time now,” he added.

Behind him, some 48,000 square meters of military infrastructure and logistics facilities had been erected by the Polish forces in the thick mud and rain, as part of the first major exercise by the Multinational Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), a non-Nato European military force, led by France and the United Kingdom, which is to be ready to deploy to Ukraine once a ceasefire has been announced.

Named Koalicja (coalition in Polish), the exercise had attracted scores of journalists, some as far away as Japan, as well as high-ranking officials and defence ministers from Estonia, France, Lithuania, Poland, and the United Kingdom.

With its 2,800 troops and jet fighter flybys of French Rafales, British RAF Typhoons, and Tiger helicopters, the MNF-U intends to provide reassurance for a Ukraine that was itself pounded overnight by a large-scaled Russian air barrage, targeting bridges in Kyiv and killing at least eight people.

]]> Rwanda return hubs may violate EU human rights law, MEPs warn ahead of 2027 deportations https://euobserver.com/250370/meps-invite-legal-challenge-to-rwanda-deportations-as-eu-states-prepare-to-expel-first-people-in-new-year/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:46:14 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250370 EU member states are aiming to deport rejected asylum seekers as early as 2027. But many MEPs believe that sending them to Rwanda is illegal as well as wrong.]]> Plans by five member states and Rwanda to establish a migrant return hub, as confirmed on Monday (16 November), could be in violation of EU human rights obligations – and liberal and leftwing MEPs are asking the European commission to review its legality.

On Monday (23 November), at least 40 MEPs from the Greens/EFA, the Left, Socialists and Democrats, and liberal Renew, will write to the EU Commission to express concerns Rwanda may be unable to fulfil key conditions under Europe’s return regulation. 

They are worried about international human rights standards being applied toward any people who might end up being hosted in Rwandan return hubs.

In 2023, the UK’s Supreme Court blocked migrant transfers to the east African nation on the basis of human rights concerns and the principle of non-refoulement.

Despite no agreement having yet being signed with Kigali, leaders and ministers from Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands announced in Vienna last Monday that a “partnership” had been agreed.

Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, joined them in Austria to say human rights concerns were founded on “cliches.”

Read more

Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret

The group met amid outstanding technical issues, with deportations to mainland Africa’s most densely populated country expected to start in 2027.

Migrants from as far afield as Afghanistan could end up in Rwanda, a country most of them would have no connection to, if their asylum applications were rejected in the EU and they do not voluntarily comply with a return order. 

Right-wing and far-right groups in the European Parliament rammed through the return regulation, which broadly mandates deportations, in June.

A letter by 22 EU leaders in August also urged the acceleration of the process after the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in north Africa in July. 

Guardian of the treaties

Inscribed as a political footnote, the caveat on human rights monitoring in the return regulation is still to be seen working in practice, but MEPs still aim to hold the commission to its obligations as guardian of European treaties, in which it monitors the implementation of EU laws.

]]> ‘Fight for our future, not their wars’: youth protests sweep across Europe https://euobserver.com/250280/fight-for-our-future-not-their-wars-youth-protests-sweep-across-europe/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:39:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250280 Youth movements took to the streets of Europe's cities on Friday. Organised across the continent, they demand more government spending on education, welfare and action in curbing high housing costs.]]> Europe’s young people from more than 20 countries across the continent took to the streets on Friday (20 November), joining forces in an International Youth Strike demanding a future built around education, housing and welfare rather than militarisation and war.

Under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars“, more than 50 separate youth organisations joined the initiative, creating the biggest coordinated European youth protest in recent years.

“We need a better education, we need housing, we need measures to deal with the rising cost of living,” Alessandro Di Miceli, an Italian organiser, told EUobserver.

The movement demands that money currently being spent on militarisation and rearmament be redirected towards education and welfare.

The strike is the result of months of organising. According to Di Miceli, organisations from around ten countries began coordinating in June, before the recent wave of youth demonstrations and labour unrest across Europe that spread across the continent over the summer.

Read more

Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down

The forms of protest on Friday differ across countries, with some organising demonstrations and marches, while others will hold actual strikes.

“The different modalities are due also to the fact that country by country, the political context is different. Also, mobilisation tactics that are used are also historically different,” said Di Miceli.

]]> Russian cruise missiles land in Poland, drones explode over EU diplomats in Kyiv (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,730) https://euobserver.com/250305/russian-cruise-missiles-land-in-poland-drones-explode-over-eu-diplomats-in-kyiv-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1730/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:44:24 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250305 With bridges shattered, power cut and ships burning off EU coasts, this latest Russian barrage also turns Ukraine’s struggle into a direct test of safety for millions of Europeans and the trade routes they rely on. ]]>
  • Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders.
  • Russian missiles damaged three Kyiv bridges, power outages hit several areas, people died at a railway station in Lviv, and a drone exploded above the Slovak EU ambassador to Ukraine.
  • There is nowhere to hide, the Russians are attacking everywhere, a Slovak diplomat wrote from Lviv.
  • Russians are sinking ships off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts.
  • The railway section of the Crimean Bridge was hit where the arch joins the pier.
  • Ukrainian pressure towards Velyka Novosilka continues.
  • The Ukrainian army has halted the formation of new brigades.
  • Maps of the day — Velyka Novosilka
  • Videos of the day — Russian weapons in Poland; a Russian drone over central Kyiv; the Russian air force receives another Su-57, while a Ukrainian pilot suggests it is not a new aircraft; HIMARS in action; a Ka-52 helicopter repelling an attack on the Crimean Bridge.

    • Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk convened a state security council after Russian weapons entered Polish territory during a massive Russian air raid on western Ukraine. According to the latest information, these were two Kh-101 cruise missiles and one drone.

    “We know for certain that we are dealing with Russian devices. It appears to be a deliberate provocation,” Tusk said.

    “It is difficult to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincided with an exercise by the coalition of the willing in Nowa Dęba,” deputy prime minister and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote.

    “This is a dangerous incident — it is a consequence of Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine,” Nato secretary general Mark Rutte added.

    The drones landed in the east of the country, in Molodych and Rudnik nad Sanem in the Podkarpackie region, as well as in Nowy Lipowiec in the Lublin voivodeship.

    This was not a minor airspace violation that could simply be brushed aside. Rudnik nad Sanem is 80 km from the Ukrainian border as the crow flies.

    ]]>         Burnham hails UK-EU reset on food, carbon markets and youth mobility, after Brexit ‘decade of drift’ https://euobserver.com/250317/burnham-hails-uk-eu-reset-on-food-carbon-markets-and-youth-mobility-after-brexit-decade-of-drift/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:37:12 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250317 There was plenty of warmth on display at an EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday. The agreements on carbon emissions, food and youth mobility could form the foundation for a decade of closer EU-UK integration.]]> The ‘reset’ deal between the EU and UK ends “a decade of drift and division”, UK prime minister Andy Burnham told reporters on Friday (20 November), after concluding a series of pacts with the EU at a summit in Brussels.

    “It is in tune with public opinion,” said Burnham, referencing recent opinion polls suggesting that 75 percent of Britons favour closer ties with the EU and “want a better deal than the hard Brexit they were given.” 

    At the heart of the new agreements are food, youth mobility and carbon markets.

    The Youth Experience Scheme (YES) will allow 100,000 young people from the EU to live in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa. This comes in addition to the UK’s participation in Erasmus+ from 2027, agreed at the first Brexit reset summit in May 2025.

    “Brexit did take opportunity away from young people,” said Burnham, noting that they had been the biggest single losers from the UK’s EU exit.

    “We missed [British Erasmus students in the EU] so much,” said EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen. “The spirit of our cooperation is win-win”.

    Agreements on carbon emissions trading and food and agriculture, meanwhile, align EU and UK laws.

    Harmonising rules on emissions trading will also give the EU and UK mutual exemptions from their carbon border taxes.

    ]]>         Estonia’s border closure makes Russia pay a price for alleged arson, as sabotage attacks spread across the EU https://euobserver.com/249994/estonias-border-closure-makes-russia-pay-a-price-for-alleged-arson-as-sabotage-attacks-spread-across-the-eu/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:29:36 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249994 After eight Latvians were caught allegedly trying to burn down an Estonian drone maker, Tallinn’s swiftly decided to close its border with Russia.]]> Estonia decided on Friday (20 November) to close all land border crossings with Russia from 1 December, in response to ongoing acts of sabotage across Europe.

    “Russia’s hostile actions have consequences. This is not a response to a single incident, but to Russia’s continued aggression, sabotage and hybrid operations targeting Estonia and Europe,” said the foreign affairs minister Margus Tsahkna.

    “We are protecting not only Estonia’s security, but also that of the European Union and the Schengen area,” he added.

    The move was announced earlier this month, following an attempted arson attack on a drone manufacturing plant on 14 November.

    Prime minister Kristen Michal said that the recent break-in at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia’s “wider hybrid war against Europe”.

    According to Estonia’s security service, Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, ordered the attack.

    On Monday, Moscow described the accusation as “unsubstantiated” and accused the Estonian government of “building a wall” between neighbouring countries.

    This was the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company in the space of several months that Estonia has attributed to Russia.

    What happened over the weekend, and why is Estonia responding to Russian attacks differently from most European countries?

    A coordinated operation

    Early last Saturday, several people smashed windows at the premises of Threod Systems, a company in the town of Viimsi that manufactures long-range strike and reconnaissance drones. Its website lists Ukraine and Nato member states among its customers.

    The attackers then poured flammable liquids into the building.

    However, a security guard spotted them and immediately called the police.

    As the investigation is being conducted in secrecy, little is yet known about the planned attack. Estonian media reported that this was not a chance discovery but a coordinated operation by Latvian and Estonian security services.

    Agents from Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD) had obtained advance information about the planned sabotage and passed it to Estonia’s internal security service, KAPO. Thanks to cooperation between the two services, Estonian police detained all eight suspects that same night. All are Latvian nationals.

    Margo Palloson, head of Estonia’s internal security service, said that Russia was behind the attempted attack and that Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, had coordinated the entire operation.

    “This was another attempt by Russia to carry out sabotage in Estonia,” he added, saying that had it gone exactly as the attackers planned, it “would have caused the company very serious damage”.

    Importers and EU producers will also get two more years to report the methane intensity of the fossil fuels they sell in the EU, now from 5 August 2030. 

    The agreement settled halfway between an earlier compromise by member states, which wanted a one-year delay earlier this month, and parliament, which voted for a three-year delay in October.

    But gone was the option, pushed by member states, to extend the delay again. Centre-left MEPs had warned it could be used to postpone the rules indefinitely, after centre-left MEPs pushed back against it, warning that it could be used to delay the rules one more time after 2029, or keep postponing them for ever. 

    Instead, the commission will only look at how the law is being implemented at the start of 2028 and whether there is any risk to security of supply. 

    And any further delay would need a whole new methane law, which came as some relief to campaigners. 

    “Despite the delay, the integrity of the regulation is preserved in the final deal,” said Léa Pilsner of Environmental Defense Fund Europe in Brussels, adding that governments had “bought themselves two years the regulation never needed”.

    But Pilsner also said 24 billion cubic metres of methane will leak into the atmosphere during the extra two-year delay, which equals two-thirds of what France uses in gas in a year. 

    Governments said the delay was needed due to supply risks and worries over high fuel prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted Gulf oil and gas supplies.

    “We are not suspending the Methane Regulation; we are ensuring that it can be effectively implemented,” said Greek centre-right MEP Dimitris Tsiodras, who led the talks for parliament’s environment committee. 

    His Polish centre-right colleague, Borys Budka, the lead MEP for the industry committee, said that “security of supply comes first”.

    Meanwhile, the cost of adapting fuel infrastructure to align with EU rules is relatively low. 

    Modelling by Rystad Energy in Oslo puts the cost of the rules at a few euro cents per million British thermal units, or about 0.3 percent of the current gas price. 

    And the International Energy Agency in Paris, in its most recent projections, sees overseas gas markets remaining tight next year, it still expects a gas glut to arrive relatively soon, due to a very large increase in gas export capacity, primarily in the United States.

    A separate analysis by Data Desk, commissioned by the European Climate Foundation in The Hague, found in September that some central and eastern European countries reliant on Russian gas could face supply challenges, but also argued that “in no case are these sufficient to disrupt the implementation of the regulation in its current form”.

    Thursday’s decision to delay follows an intense and years-long campaign led by US president Donald Trump administration and the oil and gas industry. 

    Internal commission documents, reported by EUobserver earlier this month, showed how the commission tried to placate Washington with technical fixes, while US officials and industry lobbied national capitals directly.

    Seven of the eight central and eastern European member states courted by Trump’s energy officials at a Washington summit in February later backed a three-year delay.

    Parliament is due to vote on the deal next week, and member states still need to formally sign off before the end of the year, when the original rules are due to otherwise kick in.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Earlier this week, the European Commission stepped up its action against Chinese online marketplace Temu. It announced that the platform was once again in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), and could face further fines.

    Is the EU finally managing to rein in the tech giants?

    The commission first opened an investigation into Temu in October 2024. It was looking into several issues: the sale of illegal products, potentially addictive design, the way the platform recommends products to users, and the lack of access to data for researchers.

    In May this year, the commission fined Temu €200mln. The reason? The platform had failed to properly assess the risks associated with its services, particularly the likelihood of consumers encountering illegal products.

    And on 17 November, the commission announced new preliminary findings. This time, the problem is not just that Temu failed to assess the risks. It’s that it has also failed to put effective measures in place to address them.

    The commission points to inadequate product checks, weak content moderation and an ineffective system for sanctioning sellers.

    Read more

    EU Commission again rebukes Temu over failure to stop illegal product sales, exposing Chinese giant to another hefty fine

    In other words, illegal and unsafe products are still making their way onto the platform. Temu can still respond to these preliminary findings, and no new fine has been imposed at this stage.

    But beyond Temu, is the Digital Services Act actually delivering results? Since 2024, the commission has imposed three fines under the DSA: one on Elon Musk’s social network X, one on Temu, and one on AliExpress.

    That’s a total of €870mln in fines. And that’s only part of the picture. The commission has also opened investigations into more than a dozen issues involving major platforms. Some are still ongoing, while others have ended after platforms made legally binding commitments to change their practices.

    So the fact that some investigations have been settled through commitments is already a sign that the system can work. Platforms sometimes agree to change their practices before the commission even reaches a final decision.

    And when it comes to fines, the enforcement mechanism is clearly being used. Even if the process can be rather slow, and sometimes imperfect. 

    Now, what changes did DSA bring to platforms? Take TikTok, for example. The commission launched an investigation into its potentially addictive design, including features that encourage users to spend more time on the app.

    In 2024, after the commission raised concerns about TikTok Lite’s rewards programme, the platform agreed to permanently withdraw it from the EU.

    Read more

    Consumers pay the price for online manipulation, and the EU Digital Fairness Act can put a stop to it

    That’s a concrete change. But the broader issue of addictive design is far from settled. In February this year, the commission issued preliminary findings that TikTok’s design itself could breach the DSA.

    Then there’s X. In December 2025, the platform was fined €120mln over three issues: its misleading blue verification checkmark, its lack of transparency around advertising, and its failure to provide researchers with access to public data.

    Since then, X has taken steps to address some of these issues. It has introduced a dedicated procedure for researchers who want access to public data, with a catalogue of available data and instructions on how to apply.

    But that doesn’t necessarily mean that access is now working smoothly in practice. And the blue checkmark issue also needs some nuance: in the EU, it is no longer supposed to be understood as proof that someone’s identity has been verified. It essentially signals a Premium subscription.

    These are rather easy issues to solve. What about the more delicate ones? Just look at Temu. Despite investigations and a 200-million-euro fine earlier this year, the commission still believes that illegal and unsafe products are being offered on the platform.

    Read more

    EU should use Digital Services Act against online tormentors of Belarusian and Russian exiles in Europe

    That doesn’t mean the DSA is useless. The battle is ongoing, and every commitment or change that can be secured is worth having. Whenever a platform is fined, there is criticism that the amount is too small compared with its global turnover. Under the DSA, fines can reach up to 6 percent of a company’s worldwide annual turnover.

    And in X’s case, there was also debate about whether the commission had deliberately kept the fine relatively low to avoid provoking Donald Trump and risking political or economic retaliation.

    The commission rejects that interpretation. It says its calculations are based on objective criteria, including the seriousness and duration of the infringements, and their impact on users.

    To conclude, having those tools is one thing. Making sure they actually change how these companies operate is another.

    ]]>         The same EU Parliament that built the Ethics Body is now killing it, in violation of European law https://euobserver.com/249922/the-eu-parliament-that-built-the-ethics-body-is-now-killing-it-in-violation-of-european-law/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 09:20:58 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249922 Two and a half years after signing the agreement, the EU Parliament is blocking its own ethics body before it has met even once, but EU law does not allow it to walk away so easily, and nor should parliament president Metsola.]]> No EU institution did more than the European Parliament to bring about the Union’s first common Ethics Body. Decades of scandals, from the resignation of the Santer Commission in 1999 to Qatargate in 2022, had exposed conflicts of interest, revolving doors, and the influence of private interests.

    In response, the parliament championed an unprecedented attempt to reform the fragmented and largely self-policed ethics systems of the EU institutions. It pushed for the body, negotiated its creation, approved the agreement and signed it, but today, it is the same institution quietly killing it.

    Two and a half years after the agreement was signed, the Interinstitutional Body for Ethical Standards has yet to hold its first meeting. It was presented as a landmark step towards restoring public trust in the EU.

    The political families that make up parliament’s right-wing majority are now deliberately preventing it from starting work: the European People’s Party (EPP), together with the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), Patriots for Europe (PfE), and Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) groups.

    The story began long before Qatargate, arguably the most damaging corruption scandal in the history of European integration. After the Santer commission collapsed, commission vice-president Neil Kinnock proposed an advisory group on standards in public life. The initiative was later quietly shelved.

    Academia and civil society subsequently revived the idea. In 2019, Daniel Freund, a former Transparency International EU campaigner newly elected as a German Green MEP, helped secure commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s commitment to a common independent ethics body in her political programme.

    In 2020, the Greens in the European Parliament asked me to develop a legal blueprint for such a body, drawing on France’s High Authority for Transparency in Public Life. Parliament adopted that blueprint in September 2021. It called for an independent body with investigative powers and the power to recommend sanctions.

    Yet it took Qatargate, which erupted in December 2022, to turn this long-standing proposal into an institutional priority. The scandal exposed the vulnerability of a system in which EU institutions largely policed their own members.

    Read more

    Socialist leader accuses EPP of ‘allying with far-right’ on new EU ethics body

    More critically, it unveiled how in the EU Parliament, seven in 10 MEPs have outside activities , and roughly a quarter are paid for them, under limited scrutiny.

    The pressure to show that the EU was serious about cleaning up its act became irresistible: Within a week, Parliament voted by 541 to two to demand the ethics body.

    When the EU Commission presented its proposal in June 2023, parliament called it “unsatisfactory” and pushed for a stronger role for independent experts and closer scrutiny of declarations of interest.

    Negotiations among eight EU institutions and bodies eventually produced a compromise. It fell far short of parliament’s original vision, but was still a significant achievement.

    The body would develop common minimum standards on financial and non-financial interests, outside activities, gifts, hospitality, travel, and contacts with lobbyists. Five independent experts would advise the participating institutions. Each institution would assess its own rules against the common standards and explain publicly how it intended to close the gaps.

    On 25 April 2024, MEPs approved the deal by 301 votes to 216. Three weeks later, it was signed in parliament’s name.

    EU parliament president Roberta Metsola called it “a starting point”. The text is not just a declaration of good intentions, but – as it states plainly – it is binding.

    How the EPP stalled it

    For its part, the EPP never liked it. Most of its MEPs had voted against the deal, and, after the 2024 EU elections, the party found the allies it needed to stall it: the three groups to its right.

    Read more

    Far-right opposed EU ethics body to fight corruption

    In February 2025, parliament told its partners it could not move until it had updated its internal rules. In May, the EPP and its allies voted down the very report that would have made those amendments.

    Now even the appointment of the body’s five independent experts has become a battleground.

    The Irish EU Council presidency has formally asked the EU Parliament to endorse the nominees and attend a first meeting in December.

    They are Věra Jourová, Erkki Liikanen, Leo Brincat, Dagmar Roth-Behrendt, and Élisabeth Morin-Chartier. Every other participating institution has approved them, including the EU Commission.

    Yet the EPP has blocked a fast-track endorsement in parliament. Lóránt Vincze, the EPP’s lead MEP on the file, now says the Ethics Body “cannot be revived”.

    But it has never met only because his own party blocked it.

    Parliament is still legally bound

    Slow-walking the Ethics Body, however, runs into one obstacle: EU law. Parliament formed the body by a plenary vote, and only another plenary vote can undo it.

    No political group, committee or Conference of Presidents can do so by stalling. The agreement is legally binding, and its text says so explicitly. Parliament remains bound by it unless it lawfully withdraws, and must cooperate in good faith with the other institutions that signed it.

    By refusing to take the steps necessary to make the agreement operational, the EU Parliament risks exposing itself to legal action for failure to act.

    Under Article 265 of TFEU [EU treaty], another EU institution, or a member state can formally call on parliament to act and, if it fails to define its position within two months, bring the matter before the EU Court of Justice in Luxembourg.

    The EU’s only directly elected institution could thus find itself condemned by its own court for failing to honour a commitment it voluntarily undertook.

    And where, in all this, is the parliament’s president? Metsola signed the agreement. She chairs the Conference of Presidents and, under parliament’s rules of procedure, is the institution’s legal representative. She cannot treat the agreement as a political project her own party is free to abandon. Her responsibility is to ensure that parliament honours its commitments.

    If the EPP wants out, it must make its case to the plenary, where it can be debated and voted on openly.

    How can the president allow a group of MEPs to walk away from parliament’s legal obligation without even putting it to a vote? That this group happens to be her own political family makes her silence all the harder to explain.

    MEPs are entitled to oppose the Ethics Body. They are not entitled to kill it through manufactured procedural delays that evade public scrutiny and accountability.

    Paradoxically, MEPs have remarkably little to fear from this agreement. Even the EPP, the group with the highest share of MEPs declaring paid outside activities, should not be afraid.

    The body has no power to investigate or sanction MEPs. It does not replace parliament’s own rules. It sets common standards and brings independent expertise into a system that has long relied on self-regulation.

    If even this modest step towards accountability is unacceptable, the real question is whether parliament is willing to accept even the most basic common standards of probity.

    Those who want to kill the Ethics Body should say so openly, put the EU Parliament’s withdrawal to a plenary vote, and defend that decision before European voters. Their refusal to do so tells us everything.

    They know what voters would think of MEPs who voted down an ethics watchdog, so they prefer to work in the dark. It is now up to Metsola, and the rest of us, to drag the situation into the light.

    ]]>         EU should tax Big Tech and crypto to help farmers in next budget, Spanish socialist MEP says https://euobserver.com/249143/eu-should-tax-gambling-and-crypto-to-help-farmers-in-new-budget-spanish-socialist-mep-says/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:56:53 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249143 As EU leaders wrangle over Europe’s next long-term budget, socialist MEP Sandra Gómez López warns that unless Big Tech, online gambling, and crypto start paying more, farmers and poorer regions will be the ones footing the bill.]]> Europe’s next long-term budget may seem far removed from everyday life. Yet the decisions being debated in Brussels will shape the support available to our farmers, investment in our regions, and Europe’s ability to respond to an increasingly uncertain world.

    The European Commission’s proposal for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) would significantly change both the structure of the budget and the balance between its priorities, shifting resources from policies such as cohesion and agriculture towards security and competitiveness.

    The European Parliament recognises that changing circumstances require a different budget.

    Europe needs the means to deliver what it promises to its citizens and businesses.

    But we cannot finance every new priority by cutting another. Cohesion and agriculture deliver tangible benefits across Europe.

    Asking the people who depend on them to bear the cost of new responsibilities is a political choice, not an inevitability.

    There is a way forward: genuine new sources of revenue for the EU budget. As negotiations advance, European leaders must give this question the same attention as the debate over spending.

    Read more

    Cut the EU budget and we all lose

    Own resources in practice

    “Own resources” may sound like Brussels jargon. The question behind it is straightforward: how do we pay for what Europe needs?

    Some member states want to cut the commission’s proposed budget, while others believe it already falls short of what Europe needs to meet its challenges.

    New own resources could help break this deadlock by funding our common priorities without relying solely on higher national contributions.

    The aim is to bring in at least €60bn a year for the next EU budget.

    We must repay the money borrowed together under NextGenerationEU to help our economies and societies recover from the pandemic.

    We must also fund the responsibilities we are asking the EU to take on.

    Without new revenue, these demands will place further pressure on existing programmes and national budgets.

    That is why an agreement on new own resources must go hand in hand with the next MFF.

    Read more

    Von der Leyen joins MEPs in defence of EU’s €2 trillion spending plan ahead of summit

    Where should the money come from?

    The EU Parliament proposes levies on digital services, online gambling and crypto-assets. These would complement the Commission’s proposed basket of revenues, rather than replace it.

    That basket includes a contribution from large companies operating in the EU, known as Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE); a tobacco excise duty-based own resource (TEDOR); a revised share of revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS); revenue from the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); and a contribution based on non-collected electronic waste, intended both to raise revenue and to encourage better collection and recycling.

    Read more

    [Interview] Czech MEP Niedermayer slams Babiš opposition to new EU budget revenue: ‘It’s short-sighted’

    Parliament’s proposals broaden the options available for reaching an agreement.

    They would help finance our common priorities while limiting the pressure to increase national contributions or cut programmes.

    Why Big Tech, gambling, and crypto

    Large multinational companies earn substantial revenues from Europe’s digital market. It is only fair that they contribute to the public investment and shared prosperity that help sustain it.

    Some member states already apply digital services taxes. Their experience provides a starting point for action at European level.

    For online gambling and betting, there is also a compelling social argument. Addiction carries a cost for those affected, their families and the public services that respond to its consequences.

    It is only fair that an industry profiting from this activity should help bear that cost. Existing national taxes provide a basis for a coordinated European approach that would also generate revenue for the EU budget.

    Crypto-assets also deserve attention. As governments work to address the challenges of this relatively new sector, a levy on its profits could provide another source of revenue.

    A common approach would help avoid a patchwork of national measures.

    These proposals reflect a simple principle: sectors that benefit from the European market should make a fair contribution to its future.

    Take MEPs’ proposals seriously

    National governments have a central role in shaping the next long-term budget, but the European Parliament’s consent is also essential.

    Reaching an agreement will require a shared effort. For us in the Socialists and Democrats Group, genuine new own resources are an essential part of that agreement.

    European leaders cannot keep asking the Union to do more while refusing to discuss how to pay for it. Nor should farmers, local communities, and families be left to absorb the cost through cuts to the policies they rely on.

    Those who earn substantial profits from our single market must also contribute. That is the choice at the heart of this budget debate.

      <description><p>Union leaders from 19 countries urge reassessment of ties to Amazon, citing company’s poor record on worker rights</p><p>More than 30 labor union leaders from 19 countries are calling on governments to review their public contracts with Amazon and Amazon Web Services, citing the company’s poor record on worker rights and collective bargaining, in an<a href="https://uniglobalunion.org/wp-content/uploads/Amazon-procurement-letter-embargoed-until-nov-19.pdf"> open letter</a> published on Thursday.</p><p>“Amazon’s consistent record of disrespect for workers’ fundamental rights should disqualify it from being awarded public contracts – its behaviour is fundamentally inconsistent with the shared democratic values of our countries,” the union leaders wrote.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/nov/19/labor-unions-amazon-contracts-open-letter">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/19/trump-lawsuit-new-york-times</link>
      <description><p>Trump alleges defamation by three Times reporters and Penguin Random House in campaign against news outlets</p><p>A federal ⁠judge in Florida on Thursday said Donald Trump’s<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/sep/16/donald-trump-says-he-is-suing-new-york-times-15bn-lawsuit-against-newspaper-ntwnfb"> $15bn defamation lawsuit </a>against the New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory ⁠for the US president in his ⁠legal campaign ​against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.</p><p>US district judge Steven Merryday in Tampa dismissed two claims in the suit while allowing core defamation claims to move forward.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/19/trump-lawsuit-new-york-times">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/new-york">New York</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/media/new-york-times">New York Times</category>

      <description><p>Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy</p><p>Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday.       <description><p>Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat</p><p>From <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2020/jan/04/profumo-scandal-trial-of-christine-keeler-bbc">Profumo</a> to <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-20317995">Petraeus</a> to <a href="https://www.americanheritage.com/content/30-years-ago-gary-harts-monkey-business-and-how-candidate-got-caught">Gary Hart</a>, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-bill-gates-relationship-with-jeffrey-epstein-as-he-is-interviewed-in-house-probe">Bill Gates</a> and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/clinton">Bill Clinton</a>, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 20 Nov 2026 20:54:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Paddy McKillen jnr creditors offered €445,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/paddy-mckillen-jnr-creditors-offered-445000/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/paddy-mckillen-jnr-creditors-offered-445000/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:34:15 +0000Creditors owed €27 million by Paddy McKillen jnr would get €445,000 in a proposed settlement backed by a contribution of €500,000 from his brother Tyrone, it has emerged.

McKillen jnr’s pub, restaurant and hotel empire collapsed in the fallout from Covid and under pressure from rising interest rates, leaving him on the hook for personal guarantees over many of its debts.

A personal insolvency arrangement offers to distribute €445,472 to creditors owed €27 million, in a proposal tabled by Eugene McDarby of UHY Personal & Corporate Insolvency Solutions Ltd.

The offer amounts to 1.9 cent on the euro, against the estimated 0.31 cent that creditors would get in a bankruptcy.

Tyrone McKillen is offering a lump sum of €500,000 to fund the deal on condition that his brother keep a 40-year-old Porsche valued at €45,000, a 1983 6 Series BMW worth €25,000, and five paintings by Patrick Gormley, worth €15,000 in total.

The cars and paintings are of sentimental value to Paddy McKillen jnr, reports noted. He would keep a Volkswagen Golf needed for daily family use.

McKillen jnr would also retain his family home on Torquay Road, Foxrock, Dublin, valued at €2.475 million.

The Foxrock property is held on trust for himself, his mother Maura McKillen, who is owed €1.6 million, and siblings Tyrone, Kali and Dean, while Bank of Ireland has a mortgage of €734,000 secured against it.

After any sale, the debts due to the bank and Maura McKillen most be paid first, followed by the rest of the family. Once those liabilities are cleared, McKillen jnr’s own interest amounts to €22,000.

McKillen jnr owes his creditors €29.9 million, but €2.9 million is due to his wife, Ellen McKillen, who is not seeking a dividend.

He has no income barring a €1,300 monthly contribution from his wife. The couple have four children.

The biggest single creditor is lender Cabriz finance, which is due €10.8 million.

Creditors will vote on the proposal at a meeting on December 3rd, the day before High Court protection given to McKillen jnr in September ends.

However, that meeting will not proceed if the High Court sets aside the protection to allow creditors Cabriz and Herbert Street Property Finance to cross-examine McKillen jnr on his financial affairs.

The court heard their applications last week and has reserved judgment.

Both raised concerns about what they alleged were material non-disclosures in information that he provided in his application for a personal insolvency arrangement.

McKillen jnr dismissed the claims, saying they were designed to exert maximum pressure on him to force a settlement.

Introduced by legislation in 2012, personal insolvency arrangements allow people who cannot repay their debts to restructure those liabilities over periods of up to six years.

]]>Collins Photos<![CDATA[Barry O’Callaghan’s Cliff at Lyons estate bought by hospitality group Ardán Collective]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/barry-ocallaghans-cliff-at-lyons-estate-bought-by-hospitality-group-ardan-collective/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/barry-ocallaghans-cliff-at-lyons-estate-bought-by-hospitality-group-ardan-collective/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:37:29 +0000Ardán Collective, a Dublin-based independent hospitality group with a portfolio of hotels across Ireland and Britain, has acquired the Cliff at Lyons estate in Co Kildare from businessman Barry O’Callaghan.
