]]><![CDATA[Anthropic shares fall as tech stocks slump]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/anthropic-shares-fall-as-fears-over-ai-boom-dominate/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/anthropic-shares-fall-as-fears-over-ai-boom-dominate/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:04:42 +0000

Anthropic’s shares tumbled back to their initial public offering (IPO) price and US stocks slumped on Friday, amid growing investor fears over the durability of the AI boom.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 had fallen 3.9 per cent by early afternoon in New York, taking it to more than 18 per cent below its recent peak. The S&P 500 dropped 2.3 per cent, pushing the blue-chip index more than 10 per cent below its October peak into so-called correction territory.

Shares in Claude maker Anthropic, which had surged 17 per cent on Thursday on its first day of trading, tumbled 14 per cent as a weeks-long sell-off in tech stocks gathered pace. Its shares, which were sold at $83 in its initial public offering, fell back to that price by around lunchtime in New York on Friday.

The listing was billed as a defining moment for the artificial intelligence (AI) industry and global markets, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to one of the world’s leading developers of the technology.

But investors said Anthropic’s assured first day of trading had not been enough to allay mounting fears over the sustainability of the increasingly debt-fuelled AI boom.

“The [market] psychology is fairly broken at this stage,” said one senior equities banker. Investors “were hoping for the IPO to be a clearing event” but “people are still worried about AI capex and data centre build in the US”, they added.

Anthropic’s Irish staff poised to benefit from IPO following €8.4m share awards

Anthropic said on Friday that its underwriters had exercised the so-called “greenshoe” option to buy another $12.2 billion (€11 billion) worth of shares at the original $83 IPO price.

It also closed a $26 billion private placement led by Nvidia and Google. That took the IPO’s total proceeds to about $119.5 billion, including returns from shares sold by existing investors but before fees and expenses.

Anthropic pressed ahead with its IPO despite the Democrats’ victory in this month’s US midterm elections deepening the challenge for the AI sector, after the rapid expansion of data centres became a flashpoint for voters.

“Normally, the biggest IPOs are done at the peak of the market, not at the bottom,” said Hao Hong, chief investment officer for Lotus Asset Management, referring to Anthropic’s listing.

Seb Barker, chief market strategist at hedge fund firm Marshall Wace, said of the slide in tech stocks: “We think this price action is overdone and we’ve now entered irrational ‘panic’ territory, but it’s hard to have high short-term conviction.”

The sell-off hit global markets on Friday. In Asia, South Korea’s Kospi and Japan’s Nikkei 225 both lost more than 5 per cent, and the Stoxx Europe 600 fell 1.9 per cent.

Chipmakers were among the biggest casualties in the US market. Sandisk dropped 16 per cent and Western Digital and Micron were both down around 13 per cent. Nvidia fell 7 per cent.

Dec Mullarkey, head of investment strategy and asset allocation at SLC Management, said: “Markets are worried that for Anthropic to sustain its valuation, it needs to transform the old order, resulting in casualties.”

In a sign of the broader souring in risk appetite, Government bonds rallied on Friday, with 10-year US Treasury yields down 0.11 points at 4.94 per cent. Yields on 10-year German Bunds fell 0.11 percentage points to 3.3 per cent. Yields move inversely to prices.

The Vix index of expected stock volatility, dubbed Wall Street’s “fear gauge”, hit 31, double the recent low touched in September and its highest level since the market turmoil sparked by the start of the Iran war.

The prospect of interest rates heading even higher has also had a chilling effect on the AI trade. Minutes from the October meeting of Federal Reserve officials, which were published on Wednesday, showed the debate at the US central bank had shifted to raising rates further, threatening the financing for the AI capex boom.

Bitcoin tumbled below $60,000 for the first time since July and gold was down more than 2 per cent as the selling spread to other asset classes on Friday.

The declines in global tech stocks mark a sharp reversal for what had been some of the world’s best performers since the start of 2025.

The unceremonious departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia and the prospect of tightening US restrictions on chip exports had already dented investor sentiment for the chipmakers crucial to the global AI data centre buildout.

“The public markets have been driven by narratives for a while now and the biggest narrative just got smacked on the face,” said Nikhil Srinivasan, portfolio manager at Singapore-based Benzaiten Macro. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Charly Triballeau<![CDATA[Global shares decline as investors struggle to keep confidence in banking and AI]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/global-shares-decline-as-investors-struggle-to-keep-confidence-in-banking-and-ai/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/global-shares-decline-as-investors-struggle-to-keep-confidence-in-banking-and-ai/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:50:39 +0000Global shares broadly declined on Friday to close a trading week mired by controversies in the banking and technology sectors. With Anthropic’s much-billed entrance on to the stock market, the fizzling excitement is now giving way to growing concerns over the stability of artificial intelligence (AI) stocks.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index declined 2.16 per cent to close at 14,378.74, as Dublin’s banking sector and airline industry struggled to see positive results.

Bank of Ireland fell 2.87 per cent to €18.29 a share, while retailing rival AIB fared slightly better, although was still worse off by close of markets, down 2.57 per cent to €11.00 a share.

Meanwhile, other typical Iseq heavyweights saw further let downs, with building materials specialist Kingspan dropping 5.40 per cent to €91.05 and airline Ryanair dipping 2.32 per cent to €24.44.

Nutrition giant Kerry Group, however, saw its share price increase 1.19 per cent to €102.20 a share, as did housebuilder Cairn Homes, up 1.81 per cent to €2.81.

London

The London Stock Exchange ended the trading week in the red, although with notably less volatility than its European and US counterparts, brought upwards in part thanks to strong performances in popular consumer brands.

The city’s two leading indices declined, however. The blue-chip FTSE 100 decreased 1.02 per cent, while its mid-market equivalent FTSE 250 dropped 2.23 per cent by close.

Financial services saw a particular downward trend, with banks HSBC falling 3.62 per cent, Lloyds dropping 2.19 per cent and Barclays a further 3.33 per cent by close. Little change in the energy sector, with Shell maintaining its Thursday closing price and BP dipping slightly by 0.13 per cent, meant the indices were not further dragged down.

Stronger results from companies concerned with popular consumer staples, such as Coca Cola and Tesco, were a notable upward exception to the broader decline, increasing 2.13 per cent and 0.55 per cent, respectively.

Europe

Shares on European bourses fell across the board. Financial and industrial markets saw widespread collapses in share prices, driven partly by waning investor confidence in the traditionally secure sectors. The blue-chip Stoxx 50 closed 2.9 per cent lower than Thursday’s price, while its mid-market equivalent Stoxx 600 was down 2 per cent.

The banking sector in particular suffered falls in share price, with Spain’s Santander down 2.73 per cent, France’s BNP Paribas dropping 2.54 per cent and Italy’s Intesa Sanpaolo dipping 2.36 per cent by close of markets. Germany’s Deutsche Bank, however, was the worst off: declining 3.16 per cent to close a week haunted by a Financial Times investigation into the institution.

The industrial sector, too, decreased across the board.

New York

Early trades on Wall Street suffered from a bruising tech struggle that dragged US stocks towards their longest slide since 2020 as investors piled into bonds for added security.

By midday New York time, the city’s leading market indices were all in the red: the S&P seemed set for its seventh consecutive drop, down 1.7 per cent, as the Nasdaq 100 fell 3 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fared slightly better, but still 0.3 per cent worse off that Thursday’s close of markets.

Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the initial public offering is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade. – Additional reporting by Bloomberg

Santiago<![CDATA[Irish-founded software start-up Hoplite raises $5.5m in funding]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/irish-founded-software-start-up-hoplite-raises-55m-in-funding/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/irish-founded-software-start-up-hoplite-raises-55m-in-funding/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:06:32 +0000Irish-founded software start-up Hoplite has raised $5.5 million (€5 million) to develop its platform that provides an easier way for developers to run artificial intelligence coding agents in the cloud.

]]><![CDATA[Anthropic’s Irish staff poised to benefit from IPO following €8.4m share awards]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/anthropics-irish-staff-poised-to-benefit-from-ipo-following-84m-share-awards/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/anthropics-irish-staff-poised-to-benefit-from-ipo-following-84m-share-awards/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:05:31 +0000Staff at Anthropic’s Dublin operation are positioned to benefit from its record-breaking stock market flotation after the company recognised €8.4 million in share-based remuneration last year.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind Claude began trading on Wall Street on Thursday. Its shares rose 17 per cent to close at about $97 (€88) a share after it raised $81 billion in the largest-ever initial public offering.

New accounts filed on Friday by Anthropic Ireland Limited show the company’s Irish subsidiary awarded hundreds of thousands of share options and restricted stock units to employees last year.

In total, the company recognised €8.4 million in share-based remuneration for its Irish employees in 2025, compared with a €4.9 million salary bill. Salaries were equivalent to an average of about €225,000 per employee.

The filing stated Anthropic employed an average of 22 people in Ireland during the year. Its year-end headcount was higher than that figure, however, following extensive recruitment throughout 2025.

Share options granted to Irish-based employees by Anthropic give them the right to buy shares later at a set price.

Anthropic Ireland Limited said average fair value was €71.32 for each option and €94.62 for each restricted stock unit. These are accounting estimates and do not reflect the amount employees received or the value of the awards at the time of the flotation.

The accounts did not disclose how many of Anthropic’s employees received share awards or the financial rewards they would be in line to receive from the company’s initial public offering that took place on Thursday.

On Thursday, Anthropic’s stock rose as much as 39 per cent above its $83 Nasdaq listing price, which was higher than the initial target of $78, before closing at about $97 a share.

When contacted by The Irish Times, the company declined to comment.

Anthropic, which set up its Irish unit in 2024, has announced plans to develop a sizeable office in Dublin and create 200 jobs in Ireland by 2027.

Last year, the AI company’s Irish subsidiary, which sells its Claude services across Europe, generated turnover of €308.4 million, up from €27.7 million the previous year. It booked an after-tax loss of €78 million in the year, a large rise on the €9.1 million in 2024.

The latest job announcement in March came less than a year after the company revealed plans to hire more than 100 staff across Dublin and London.

By March this year, 85 staff had been hired in Ireland for its sales, legal and finance units.

Among the new recruits was Aiden Blake, a former Google executive who is now Anthropic’s head of start-up sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Siobhain Ivers, who previously held a senior role at Etsy’s Irish operation, also joined last October as head of integrity and compliance.

Blake and Ivers are considered two of the highest-ranking staff at Anthropic’s Irish office, alongside Ronan Davy, a former executive at Etsy’s Irish office, who joined Anthropic in 2024 and is now the firm’s head of regulatory legal.

This year the company has advertised dozens of jobs for its Dublin office, with salaries between €200,000 and €355,000 listed for many of the roles.

The Thursday flotation by the AI lab, led by Dario and Daniela Amodei, secured the firm a market value of $1.3 trillion at its closing price, which placed it in the elite club of companies valued above $1 trillion, but lower than SpaceX’s valuation at the end of its first day.

]]>Charly Triballeau<![CDATA[Anthropic shares skyrocket at first but slip as day goes on]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/19/anthropic-raises-81bn-in-record-ipo/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/19/anthropic-raises-81bn-in-record-ipo/Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:03:24 +0000Shares in Anthropic began trading on Wall Street on Thursday in a key test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom that has powered a multiyear bull market.

Shares opened 34.3 per cent higher at $111.50 (€101.5), according to Nasdaq data, up from their $83 initial public offering (IPO) price.

The jump gave the AI giant a market capitalisation of $2 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The listing provides a signal of investors’ continued appetite for AI after a volatile month for tech stocks.

However, as the day wore on, shares eased back, ​the stock pared gains and closed at $97.17, up 17 per cent from ‌its IPO price.

In early afternoon trading in New York, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.8 per cent, the S&P 500 was 1.4 per cent lower and the Nasdaq fell 1.4 per cent despite Anthropic’s debut.

Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, the siblings who run the company, rang Nasdaq’s opening bell.

“We will not bend to either business or political pressure,” Dario Amodei said, pledging to avoid the potentially catastrophic risk of AI by remaining “obsessed with safety”.

The group drew bumper demand for its listing as institutional and retail investors clamoured to gain exposure to one of the biggest players in the AI boom.

Anthropic’s listing also helped restore confidence in the AI trade, which has teetered in recent weeks as investors fret over the vast spending on chips and data centres powering the latest models.

]]><![CDATA[Spend your gift vouchers as soon as you get them – there’s no point in waiting ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/20/spend-your-gift-vouchers-as-soon-as-you-get-them-theres-no-point-in-waiting/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/20/spend-your-gift-vouchers-as-soon-as-you-get-them-theres-no-point-in-waiting/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:17:11 +0000Until the end of 2019, readers of The Irish Times would frequently make contact with us to complain about the ridiculous terms and conditions that were attached to the gift vouchers they had given or received.

The sector – despite being worth hundreds of millions of euro annually – was almost completely unregulated. That lack of regulation was relentlessly exploited by retailers, restaurants, hairdressers, hotels, airlines and all the rest.

They imposed all sorts of ridiculously consumer-unfriendly terms and conditions on the sale of vouchers and were happy to bury all the unfair rules deep in the T&Cs, knowing we as consumers could do nothing about it.

Vouchers were sold with expiry dates of 12 months, six months, or even less. Shops, restaurants and airlines routinely refused to give people change – even in voucher form – if they bought something for less than the full value of their voucher.

Unfortunate consumers were told they could not use their vouchers during sale periods, and retailers could refuse to accept two vouchers worth €50 each for a product or service that cost €100.

It was insane and saw hard-earned cash turn into overly complicated pieces of paper that sometimes actively worked against our best interests.

Because of the shambolic way the system operated, Irish consumers lost tens of millions of euro every year – while those who sold the vouchers to us laughed all the way to the bank.

There were attempts to fix things. In 2009, the Labour Party proposed the Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Bill, but it was rejected by the government of the day for reasons best known to itself. In 2015, then minister for enterprise Richard Bruton published a draft consumer rights Bill, which contained several provisions for the regulation of vouchers, but it never became law. And an attempt by the Social Democrats to bring another Bill before the Dáil in 2018 also foundered.

But in 2019 everything changed. Then minister for enterprise Heather Humphreys successfully got legislation over the line that imposed consumer-friendly rules on the gift voucher industry.

Profits jump 13% to €7.5m at gift card group One4All

The Consumer Protection (Gift Vouchers) Act set a minimum expiry date of five years for vouchers and banned contract terms that required them to be spent in a single transaction.

If a consumer did not redeem the full amount of the voucher in an initial purchase, businesses were required to reimburse any remaining balance of more than €1 by cash, electronic transfer or voucher.

The law also banned contract terms that limited the number of vouchers that could be used in a transaction.

In passing the legislation, Ireland became the first European country to enact laws protecting consumers in this area. However, more than six years on, some retailers appear to be struggling to come to terms with the changes.

That became clear this week when the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) said it had identified retailers doing business in the State who were not complying with the law on gift vouchers.

It was able to establish this by using recent data from consumer reports to its helpline.

Irish gift voucher legislation is clear, and traders selling vouchers must follow the law

Aoibhín de Búrca of the CCPC

It wrote to traders around the country to remind them of the rules, highlighting a number of issues and drawing attention to the core provisions of the consumer law around gift vouchers.

It called on traders who had sold vouchers valid for less than five years in the post-2019 period to engage with the CCPC and propose remedies for affected consumers.

“We are still hearing from consumers who are experiencing issues with gift vouchers,” said CCPC director of communications and consumer information Aoibhín de Búrca.

“As we approach one of the busiest times of year for the purchase and use of gift vouchers, we are reminding traders of their consumer protection obligations.”

She said: “Irish gift voucher legislation is clear, and traders selling vouchers must follow the law. The legislation is there for consumers and we want consumers to know what their rights are, and to get the full protection and value of the legislation.”

The CCPC did not name any retailers that were in breach of the law. The letter has been sent to a wide range of businesses including hotels, restaurants, takeaways, dentists, sports retailers, clothes shops, salons and spas.

Some retailers are not complying with gift voucher laws, says Irish consumer watchdog

But we know at least a couple that it may have had in mind.

In July of this year, JD Sports issued refunds of €250,000 to consumers following a CCPC investigation that came in the wake of revelations in The Irish Times that it had sold gift vouchers valid for only one year, instead of at least five years.

In recent weeks, this newspaper revealed that British fashion retailer Flannels – which is owned by Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group – had sold vouchers that came with a two-year expiry in line with its UK policies but contrary to Irish law.

It is only right that the CCPC and consumers focus on vouchers now because it will soon be Christmas, and in the weeks ahead millions of euro will be spent on these things.

Recent CCPC research has found that two-thirds of people received at least one the previous Christmas. That research highlights a problem that is beyond legislation and even retailer ignorance of the law. The blame for that other problem may rest with us: as many as one in five people who get a voucher do not spend it in the first year. There is a good chance that if a voucher is not used in the first 12 months, it will go unused forever – and that means we are wasting as much €70 million a year.

Even if we do get around to spending them eventually, we are taking a risk by waiting. The retail space is volatile and shops come and go.

Liquidators appointed to Dundrum Harvey Nichols store

Earlier this year, the Harvey Nichols store in Dundrum Town Centre closed down after the sale of its UK parent to Frasers Group through what is known as a prepack administration process in the UK. Liquidators from Grant Thornton were appointed to the Irish business.

One of the liquidators’ first actions was to post a notice on the store’s website stating that any “orders placed and gift cards purchased before August 13th, 2026, fall under the ownership structure preceding this transition”.

In other words, they were not being honoured.

When a retailer goes out of business or changes ownership as part of an insolvency process, the holders of gift cards and vouchers are ranked among unsecured creditors and are at the back of the queue when seeking payments.

By the time the secured creditors – Revenue and banks – get at least some of their debt repaid, there is rarely anything left for those unsecured creditors.

That is why it is a good idea to spend the vouchers you get as soon as you get them. There is almost no point in waiting.

]]><![CDATA[Can Bawag transform PTSB into a credible challenger to AIB and Bank of Ireland?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/ptsb-is-not-going-to-become-a-third-force-overnight-but-its-got-a-better-shot-under-bawag/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/20/ptsb-is-not-going-to-become-a-third-force-overnight-but-its-got-a-better-shot-under-bawag/Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Bawag’s shares have surged more than 50 per cent over the past 12 months, putting the Austrian group among Europe’s top-performing bank stocks, as it pursued and ultimately won the hand of PTSB.

]]><![CDATA[Who has the spending power in the Irish consumer economy? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/19/who-has-the-spending-power-in-the-irish-consumer-economy/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/19/who-has-the-spending-power-in-the-irish-consumer-economy/Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:18:16 +0000Where is the spending firepower in the Irish consumer economy?

Recent figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO) give some fascinating insights, some of them a bit surprising, into the main factor determining this – how much people are paid and how this adds up at various income levels, in different types of jobs and between men and women.

The “compensation” figures in the study include wages, salaries, bonuses, benefits in kind and other payments, pensions and social insurance paid by employers and relate to 2025.

1. Where the spending power lies

Total compensation – or earnings from work – across the economy are €165 billion. After adjusting for inflation, this is up from €96 billion in 2011, reflecting real wage rises but also a much higher population.

Self-evidently, people with higher incomes have more disposable income after paying for necessities.

But with total consumer spending, it comes down to the numbers. With average full-time incomes from work at just over €50,000, the biggest earnings total comes from those in the middle ground.

And so those earning €40,000-€60,000 are the biggest group in terms of total compensation at just under €31 billion out of €165 billion – the total figure for compensation of employees in the entire economy.

Next come those earning €60,000-€80,000, who have total earnings from work of €24.5 billion. Interestingly, the small group earning €300,000 plus contribute more than €14 billion.

This shows two things. The first is the huge total spending power in the middle ground.If you are selling cars, for example, there is a market at the top end for the €60,000-plus model – but many more people looking for a new car in the €30,000-€40,000 range.

The second is that there is a lot of spending power at the top end. The combined total, counting all earners from €120,000 up, is more than €47 billion.

Further light is thrown on this by separate figures from the Revenue Commissioners. These are not directly comparable with the CSO data because they are based not on individual earnings but on “tax units”, which include individual earners but also married couples who are jointly assessed for tax. Also, it includes all income, not just that earned from work.

It shows that the 49,700 tax units estimated to earn more than €275,000 represent 1.4 per cent of the total but earn 13 per cent of the income and pay 27.4 per cent of all income tax and USC.

By contrast, there are 834,000 earners in the €40,000-€60,000 range, representing 23 per cent of the total and earning 22 per cent of the total income.

2. Who earns most?

The CSO data gives an interesting insight into who earns most. In terms of gender, men earn 58.1 per cent of total compensation in the economy, only fractionally lower than the 58.4 per cent figure for 2019.

The highest proportion of earnings for women was in the sector that includes public administration, education and health, where 64 per cent of the total wage bill goes to women.

As female participation in the labour force has risen a bit faster than male participation, a somewhat greater rise in total female earnings might have been expected.

Female participation in Irish workforce jumps 90% since 2000

The mix of full and part-time work could be a factor here. Also, some of the biggest wage growth has been in higher-tech sectors where men hold the bulk of the jobs. In the foreign-owned sectors, 67.5 per cent of total compensation to employees was paid to men, while in other sectors it was 56 per cent.

The figures also break down earnings by age, showing – not surprisingly – that those in their peak earnings years of 40-49 were the biggest recipients of compensation from 2019 to 2025, with the figure around 30 per cent of the total over the period.

In the multinational sector, the age profile is younger, and those in their thirties received around 31 per cent of total compensation, just behind the 33 per cent taken by those in their forties. They also had much fewer earners over the age of 60.

Across the economy, those aged 60 and over contributed the least to total compensation from 2019 to 2023, but the earnings of this group are rising sharply, from €5.4 billion in 2019 to €11.3 billion last year. This illustratesnew rules and norms that mean many more people over the age of 60 are staying in the workforce. Some also do so because of inadequate pension provision.

3. Multinational earnings

There is no doubt that multinational industry – and finance – is where a lot of the bigger money is earned in Ireland. In the €200,001–€300,000 band, 36.5 per cent of total compensation was paid to employees in sectors dominated by foreign-owned multinationals.

This is well above their employment share. Total earnings in sectors dominated by multinationals stood at €26.5 billion.

Put another way, half of all the earnings made in sectors dominated by multinationals were made by people earning more than €120,000. Across the economy in other sectors, this falls to less than a quarter.

How tech workers earning six-figure salaries are changing the Dublin housing market

Meanwhile, professional, administration and support services experienced the highest growth in the share of total compensation to employees since 1995, increasing from 4.7 per cent (€1.1 billion) in 1995 to 14.6 per cent (€24.1 billion) in 2025. This includes strong growth in legal and accounting firms, where big multinationals are key clients.

4. Long-term trends

How have employee earnings kept up with economic growth over the years? Pretty well, according to the CSO, when they are measured as a percentage of modified gross national income – GNI* – the measure developed to remove the “noise” caused by multinational activity. This is probably the fairest measure.

On this basis, the figure has generally remained in the high 40 per cent over the years since 1970 and now stands at 47.5 per cent. The only time the figure went over 50 per cent was after the financial crash, when national income fell sharply, but incomes did not decline as much, on average.

When measured as a share of national income without the adjustment for multinational factors, the compensation share has fallen to below 40 per cent, highlighting, as the CSO says, the impact of Ireland’s globalised economy on economic data.

Much of this additional wealth disappears from Ireland as repatriated profits – though, of course, Ireland gets a slice of tax revenue as a result.

]]><![CDATA[After Anthropic’s public debut, will questions be asked about its unique structure?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/19/after-anthropics-public-debut-will-questions-be-asked-about-its-unique-structure/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/19/after-anthropics-public-debut-will-questions-be-asked-about-its-unique-structure/Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:45:02 +0000Todd Underwood, a former Anthropic engineering leader, fielded a stream of calls in recent months from investment managers eager to gain his insider view on the artificial intelligence (AI) giant’s business strategy before this week’s initial public offering.

But few of the questions focused on an aspect of the company Underwood viewed as a crucial asset: Anthropic’s unusual governance structure.

The company is set to become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or PBC.

That status requires Anthropic to prioritise its corporate mission – to develop safe AI systems “for the long-term benefit of humanity” – in addition to the customary sole focus on value for stockholders.

The company’s public benefit mandate is guarded partly by a five-member “long-term benefit trust”, which includes Ben Bernanke, the former Federal Reserve chair.

The company “will choose to do things in favour of safety rather than in favour of making money”, said Underwood, who has been sought out by investors as a former employee for insights into the company. He added that he agreed with that focus but thought it might turn off some investors.

The company’s public offering sets up an important test as Anthropic goes from one of the most closely watched private companies in the world to one of the most scrutinised.

Anthropic is expected to spend its first two years as a publicly traded company asking investors for patience as it burns hundreds of billions of dollars of cash to invest in new chips and data centres.

It is also facing increasing calls from AI safety advocates, as well as some of its own employees, to slow down its pace of training new models.

On Wednesday, the company is expected to sell roughly $65 billion (€59 billion) in shares, making it the second-largest IPO after SpaceX’s this year. It also has $26 billion of investments lined up from tech giants such as Nvidia and Microsoft.

Anthropic’s expected market capitalisation, more than $1.4 trillion, would make it 30 times as valuable as the next public benefit corporation that trades on the stock market, software maker Veeva Systems.

Anthropic raises $81bn in record IPO

Anthropic was founded as a public benefit corporation in 2021, and formed its long-term benefit trust in 2023 as a way to give the structure teeth, ensuring the company balances goals for shareholders and its broader mission. The structure is taxed the same as any corporation.

The trust is made up of a group of “financially disinterested” experts in economics, science and global health who do not own Anthropic stock, the company said in its offering prospectus. The group has the power to appoint and remove several of the company’s board members, authority that is typically given only to shareholders.

Adding to the unusual leadership structure, the company also spent the months leading up to its public offering locking in new authority for the executives who started the company nearly six years ago, according to securities filings.

The company created a new class of shares this fall for its unusually large co-founding team – seven executives, including chief executive Dario Amodei – that give them 50.1 per cent of voting control over the company, collectively. The founders have the ability to appoint other board members.

A founder-controlled board committee can also help overrule one of the trust’s four board appointments, reducing the trust’s power, said Jesse Fried, a Harvard University law professor who has studied Anthropic’s corporate structure.

The trust’s authority was “watered down” as a result of the changes, but they don’t “fundamentally change the governance of the company”, he added.

Anthropic’s structure is unique when compared with other publicly traded companies, corporate governance experts said.

“I don’t know if I can really compare it to anything else,” said Douglas Chia, a senior fellow at Rutgers Law School who advises companies on corporate governance. “It’s going to be an interesting experiment.”

The Council of Institutional Investors, an advocacy group that represents public, union and corporate pension funds, has long been critical of arrangements that give founders voting control disproportionate to their financial stakes. The group wrote a letter this year expressing concerns that when SpaceX went public, it gave its founder, Elon Musk, dominant voting control.

Anthropic says its AI technology ‘could pose catastrophic or existential risk to humanity’

The group will “wait and see” how Anthropic’s structure plays out, said Glenn Davis, the council’s executive director. The founders’ immense voting power means that “ultimately the founders are accountable to themselves”, rather than shareholders, he added.

The layered structure could still challenge investors’ understanding of the company and the group of people who govern it, said Paul Abrahimzadeh, a senior partner at the tech investment firm 1789 Capital.

Still, investor enthusiasm was inevitable despite the uncertainties, he added. “You have to own it. The question is at what price?” – This article originally appeared in The New York Times

Some fruit keep ripening after they have been harvested, bananas and avocados being the classic examples, but not citrus or berries. Bananas and avocados are stored by producers using “controlled atmosphere storage”.

This method keeps fruit sealed in rooms just above freezing, with oxygen levels reduced to as little as 1-3 per cent (compared to the 21 per cent in air) and elevated carbon dioxide levels. This slows down the fruit’s own metabolism and therefore ripening is practically stopped.

When shipping time approaches, the fruit is gassed with ethylene (the plant hormone that triggers ripening) so it arrives in shops nearly ready to eat. The brown-bag trick works the same way at home: the bag traps the ethylene the fruit gives off naturally.

The effect is so dramatic the fruit can be stored for months and in the case of apples even beyond 12 months. That apple you eat today might have been picked more than a year ago. – Yours, etc

]]>Kirill Kudryavtsev<![CDATA[In Ireland’s ‘no notions’ culture, how can a manager lead with and foster confidence?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/19/tap-your-inner-coach-to-build-contagious-confidence-in-your-team/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/19/tap-your-inner-coach-to-build-contagious-confidence-in-your-team/Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:01:00 +0000“Who does she think she is?” and “He’s so full of himself” are phrases many of us have heard or thought when a colleague proposed a new idea or was promoted, or even when an energetic new hire arrived.

Confidence is not something that is always culturally valued. Using American-style language like “just believe in yourself” or “go for it” will rarely get you very far as a manager.

Leadership consultant Julie Smith agrees that this type of pep talk doesn’t work. There’s not a switch where you think “Oh, okay. I hadn’t thought about being confident. Maybe I’ll do that now.”

Coldly delivered praise or rigid “stiff upper lip” work practices encountered in some British companies might not fly here either. Our workplaces are flatter and managers are supposed to be fairly equal to staff, so sometimes confidence and hierarchy can feel threatening.

Individual and team confidence building needs to be done within our more collaborative, relationship-focused and egalitarian workplaces as we place a high value on personal rapport, empathy and informal teamwork in Ireland.

In her new book, Contagious Confidence, Smith argues that confidence is an important driver of team performance but most organisations have not yet learned how to use it properly, even though it can be particularly helpful for time-poor teams.

Smith says the leaders she coaches now – after working for decades herself in the corporate world – have workloads that keep growing without adequate support. “I don’t know any leaders or any organisations where it’s a viable option to just add more resources.”

That’s where contagious confidence comes in. “A team that has this sense of ‘we’ve got this’ is going to push harder, is going to be more ambitious, is going to be more resilient than an equally capable team that doubts itself.”

How can you inject that kind of confidence into your own team?

Begin with yourself. Every leader is already spreading belief or doubt, whether they mean to or not, says Smith. A manager who has a loud inner critic, or a tendency for perfectionism, sets their team up for failure.

Why emotionally intelligent people bear the most weight in toxic workplaces

“There’s an unsaid feeling that they’re always going to be disappointed because nobody can meet their impossible standards. People pick up on that; it leaks out whether you want it to or not” she says.

The inner critic and the begrudger are close relations. Some of us still battle programming from our childhood, such as an avoidance of “getting notions” or a propensity for giving someone a backhanded compliment instead of real praise. This does not serve us well in the modern workplace.

Humble confidence

So what kind of confidence works in a culture that distrusts show-offs?

Not the loud, domineering kind and definitely not the slightly performative version. Smith prefers humble confidence which she defines as an alignment or match between how you see yourself and the reality of your skills and abilities. “I could have called that grounded confidence, but I think actually the idea of humility is quite important.”

We all have unlimited potential and acknowledging a strength is a statement of truth, not boasting. Her mantra is “I am good enough and I can be better.” That’s a version of confidence that a “no notions” culture can accept too, because it is never complete.

Leaders can build that kind of confidence less by cheerleading the team than by stepping back. Smith recommends giving people space, stretching them just a little bit further than they think they are ready for, and staying alongside them, like a good coach, as they try something new. That gives them not only new skills but unexpected proof points about themselves.

It’s good to have notions: Why the Irish culture of humility fails the psychology test

Paul Campbell, a retired senior vice-president of supply chain for PepsiCo Europe, learned this in Cork. In the book, he recalls how he spent the first part of his 28-year career in the UK, rising to vice-president responsible for 10 sites and 2,000 employees.

“I was convinced that the way to lead was to cajole people; to put my arm around them, look over their shoulder, tell them what was wrong, and give them the right answer.”

Then he moved to PepsiCo’s global concentrate business in Cork, where the manufacturing process was very different. He couldn’t show anyone what to do because he didn’t know how to do anyone’s job there. Instead, he started asking questions.

“It started with me being curious as to what they were doing. I would ask ‘what’s the problem?’ I realised that my questions were enabling people to figure things out for themselves. And it was transformational.” The change stuck. Campbell permanently set aside his helpful-expert version of leadership and used a coaching style instead.

He’s not alone in finding it hard, though. When leaders rate themselves against common leadership beliefs or behaviours and compare the results, they’ll often find that “listening more than talking” is their lowest-rated item every time, both by the leaders themselves and by their teams.

The danger of hiring a confident but incompetent employee

Stepping back can feel risky when you think you’re paid to know all the answers. Let’s say a manager has been coaching and investing in “Susan” and then she’s suddenly more engaged, confident and full of ideas. The manager now feels threatened, and Susan’s long-serving colleague, “John”, starts to act up.

Smith says the worst response is to act on that initial feeling. “If I just act on the threat then maybe I stop empowering her or I step in and do the work because that’s one way of me easing my discomfort.”

Ask yourself instead: “How can I ensure that my confidence doesn’t automatically sap somebody else’s, that it cultivates their confidence rather than the opposite?”

Nor should the manager in this scenario referee by playing mum or dad with work siblings who are squabbling.

“Think instead: how do I equip these two individuals with the skills to navigate that conflict, that discomfort, for themselves?” That means separating task conflict from relationship conflict, and building enough trust that John can celebrate Susan’s success rather than slip into a feeling of “I’m now less than her.”

Coaching John might include one pointed question: “What are they doing versus what are you doing to yourself?”

All of this takes time, which managers just don’t have. It’s not easy but Smith has seen a contagious confidence approach pay back – and give back – time and time again. Belief-building leadership like this ultimately frees up hours of managers’ time because team members are empowered to think and make decisions for themselves.

Building confidence: top tips

  1. Start with yourself. Notice your inner critic and your perfectionism before your team does.
  2. Stretch and support. Give people a task just beyond their comfort zone, then stay alongside them. Success gives them new evidence of what they can do.
  3. Ask before you tell. In your next one-to-one, aim to listen more than you talk, and let people find their own answers.
  4. Don’t be the referee. Name the difference between task conflict and relationship conflict, and help colleagues work it out between themselves.
  5. Borrow the mantra: “We are good enough and we can be better.” That’s a belief everyone can sign up to.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

At Anthropic, where artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is understandably high, the median employee now spends 20 per cent more time in meetings than a year ago.

But while AI hasn’t superseded the need for human-to-human interaction at the company, it has changed the nature of it. Namely, people are now under pressure to communicate with each other in a machine-readable way.

In an interesting report about how employment is changing inside Anthropic, the company wrote that “private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace” because it means AI agents cannot gain up-to-date context about everything that is happening. That can lead them down blind alleys.

One poor soul, whose name was on a months-old document about Claude merchandise, found that AI agents kept channelling requests to them for T-shirts and mugs, even though their job responsibilities had changed.

As a result, it is much better for work to happen in the open: agent-visible Slack channels; recorded meetings. Anthropic is not the only AI-heavy workplace to have come to this conclusion. Shopify has built an AI coding agent that lives in the company’s Slack and only works with people in open channels, for example.

What are the advantages of working this way? Tobias Lütke, Shopify’s chief executive, has argued that it creates a sort of “Lehrwerkstatt”, or “training workshop”: everyone can watch each other working with the AI tool and so learn by osmosis. “It does not require a curriculum, a training plan or a manager,” Lütke has written. “It just requires everyone’s work to be visible to the maximum extent possible.”

The more visible the work, the more information AI agents can absorb, too, of course. This raises the prospect of AI not just as a tool but as a vast sponge of corporate information, including previously uncodified “tacit knowledge” absorbed by listening in to every meeting and Slack conversation.

When human judgment is not all it’s cracked up to be

There could be efficiency gains to this. Human co-ordination has its limits, after all. Institutional knowledge and memory often exist inside different people’s heads. They can warp or erode, especially when key people leave. In contrast, a fully queryable and constantly up-to-date repository of all that knowledge could be immensely useful, especially for new starters.

But knowledge is power, and centralising it in an AI system would redistribute that power in potentially disruptive ways.

It is one thing for Anthropic to feed Claude (its own product) as much information about its organisation as possible; it would be another thing entirely for a company to cede so much power to a system it did not own.

Workers, too, would lose the monopoly on something that is currently valuable (the tacit institutional knowledge built up inside their heads).

But more than that, I suspect the biggest disadvantage of working this way would be that many people wouldn’t like it.

When the academic Ethan Bernstein studied open workplaces, he found that too much transparency led to “counterproductive inhibitions” and stifled experimentation. I can relate to this. At the Financial Times, we can choose to write our articles directly into our publishing software (which makes the work-in-progress visible to editors and colleagues) or we can write on our own devices and then copy over a finished draft. I always choose the latter.

I find it uncomfortable to work if I think someone – or something – is looking over my shoulder. And I suspect I am not the only one.

As for meetings, the pandemic caused a lot of debate about the value of impromptu work conversations sparked by chance meetings by the water cooler. Whether these informal channels are as important as their advocates claim, I doubt that the requirement for every work-related encounter to be recorded and codified for posterity would make communicating with colleagues more enjoyable.

Indeed, one danger would be that many private conversations would continue to happen – and before long the AI agents’ picture of the organisation would diverge from reality in subtle but potentially problematic ways.

That doesn’t mean more companies won’t try it. There has been a lot of talk about AI models as “black boxes” whose inner workings we cannot understand. But rather than try to make them more legible to us, we appear to be moving towards a world in which we make ourselves more legible to them. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>akinbostanci<![CDATA[My mother got an inheritance and a gift from her parents – can she reduce her tax bill?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/19/my-mother-got-an-inheritance-and-a-gift-from-her-parents-can-she-reduce-her-tax-bill/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/19/my-mother-got-an-inheritance-and-a-gift-from-her-parents-can-she-reduce-her-tax-bill/Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Q. My mother got an inheritance from her father of €301,000, and then a €77,000 gift from her mother. The tax bill seems unfair, is there anything she can do?

A. This query highlights an important feature of capital acquisitions tax (CAT). The tax on separate gifts and inheritances is not always considered in isolation, says Eoin Tobin, a solicitor, chartered tax adviser and head of private client services at law firm RDJ.

Your mother must aggregate the inheritance and the gift received from her parents when calculating tax, says Tobin. Both benefits count towards her Group A parent-to-child lifetime tax-free threshold.

Let’s start with the inheritance your mother received from her father who died in 2017. It’s the date of the death that determines the tax-free threshold and the CAT rate applicable to an inheritance, says Tobin.

Her €301,000 inheritance was below the €310,000 Group A threshold applicable in 2017. “Assuming she had no earlier benefits from her parents, no CAT was payable on that inheritance,” says Tobin.

Even though she didn’t owe CAT, she was still obliged to file a CAT return as the inheritance exceeded 80 per cent of the applicable threshold in place at the time, says Tobin.

“Revenue is increasingly focused on collecting information about gifts and inheritances, so it’s important not to overlook a filing obligation simply because no tax is payable,” he says.

The deadline for filing depends on the “valuation” date. For an inheritance, this is typically the date of the grant of probate.

Regarding the July 2024 gift of €77,000 from her mother, the earlier inheritance from her father is still relevant. Indeed, the calculation of tax requires beneficiaries to look back to relevant gifts or inheritances received since December 5th, 1991, says Tobin.

Why am I being taxed twice over on shares I inherited?

The combined benefits in this case are €301,000, and the €77,000 which is already net of the €3,000 small gift exemption. This gives €378,000 in total.

The parent/child tax-free threshold in July 2024 was €335,000. The taxable excess received over that threshold was €43,000. Taxable at 33 per cent, this gives a CAT liability of €14,190 on the 2024 gift, says Tobin.

The reader mentions that Revenue’s IT38 form, used to declare gifts or inheritances, is showing a tax liability in her case of €22,440. This doesn’t match.

One possibility is that the dates or the details of the inheritance from the father have been entered incorrectly, says Tobin. If the two benefits have been combined in a single return, that could be the problem.

“The correct approach is to complete and file two separate IT38 returns, one for each benefit as they arise in different taxable periods,” says Tobin.

The first return should relate to the inheritance from the father, showing €301,000 with no tax due, with the valuation date linked to the date of grant of probate.

I’m giving my son a €490,000 property. Can I cut tax bill by giving part of it as a loan?

The second return should relate to the gift from her mother. It should show a prior inheritance of €301,000 as an earlier Group A benefit; the net gift of €77,000 and July 2024 as the gift date.

“By separating the two benefits in this way, each return should apply the correct threshold for the relevant date, and the aggregation of the two benefits should produce the €14,190 liability,” says Tobin.

As the return for the July 2024 gift was due by October 31st, 2024, the reader’s mother should try to deal with this promptly to avoid penalties.

If the revised forms still produce the wrong figure, ask Revenue or a tax adviser to review the calculation.

Property market sources have told The Irish Times that the family has vied for the property across a number of rounds of bids in recent weeks alongside other shortlisted bidders.

The family’s company, which now lists Michelle, Deborah, Colm, David, Declan and Joseph Edward Brennan as directors, has previously acquired a number of prominent buildings in Dublin.

Grafton Street in Dublin remains world’s 18th most expensive retail destination

The hotel investor, jointly owned by affiliates of APG Asset Management and GIC, a Singaporean sovereign wealth fund, completed a €230 million deal to add the Shelbourne hotel to its portfolio in 2024.

Archer Hotel Capital previously secured permission in 2022 to expand the Conrad from 192 to 280 bedrooms, but did not proceed with the plans.

Archer Hotel Capital’s portfolio includes 13 hotels, valued at close to €3.5 billion. In 2024, the company reported that the 4,000 bedrooms that are part of its portfolio generated €369.5 million in revenue.

The most recent accounts for the operator of the Conrad Hotel showed that its revenues rose from €20.5 million to €21.3 million in 2025. In the 12-month period, operating profit at Earlsfort Centre Hotel Proprietors Limited also increased from €2.3 million to more than €4 million.

Dublin Web Summit Limited, the company that leases the building, has applied for “retention permission” (or retrospective approval) for the works.

Late last week, Cosgrave posted on X, formerly Twitter: “I’d just like to unreservedly apologise for using red paint and putting up a sign in Ireland with the words [sic] ‘Whistleblower’ on it.”

Two years ago, they decided to take matters into their own hands, and the result is DogQuest, a newly minted online marketplace that provides breeder transparency and vet-verified health information about the puppies being offered for sale on its site.

“Bad breeders thrive because buyers have very little independent information to distinguish a responsible breeder from somebody who simply knows how to write a convincing advert. We are on a mission to change this,” Moore says.

“DogQuest is not another advertising website. It’s a website that prioritises traceability, so people know who they’re buying from and whether the puppy’s health status has been verified.

“Current marketplaces allow sellers to say that a puppy has been vaccinated or health checked, but the buyer has no way of knowing whether that claim is genuine,” Moore adds. “In theory, this means I could place an ad and tick a box and even upload documentation. But who has authenticated the information?

“With AI and digital documentation, authentication becomes even more problematic. We’ve heard countless stories of puppies being handed over in car parks and buyers being told that a puppy was vaccinated only to discover it wasn’t when the puppy subsequently became seriously ill with something like parvovirus.”

In ads placed on the DogQuest website, a green tick indicates vet-verified vaccination, while a gold star signifies a vet-verified health check. “Microchip requirements already exist across the industry, but we’re trying to take trust much further by creating additional layers of authentication and traceability,” Moore says, adding that sellers can be reviewed on the site, which adds an increased level of accountability and provides responsible breeders with a way to differentiate themselves in the marketplace.

Higher fines for rogue puppy farm operators in animal welfare strategy

Getting the DogQuest system to work required buy-in from the veterinary profession, and Moore concedes that there was no easy way of doing this.

“Basically, it’s been about knocking on doors and meeting the vets face-to-face. Over the last two years Brian and I have contacted veterinary practices all over Ireland and have worked closely with 70 practices to build authentication into our marketplace. We’ve been genuinely taken aback by the overwhelmingly positive response from the veterinary community, which also wants a solution to the current problems with how puppies are sold.

“Participating vets get a unique DogQuest verification code for vaccinations and health checks. So, instead of the breeder claiming something has happened, we can verify that it has,” Moore says. “The original idea for DogQuest came from Brian, but since then it has developed into a much broader mission around puppy welfare, buyer protection, responsible breeding, education and traceability.”

Dog ownership spiked in Ireland during Covid, which exacerbated the overbreeding problem and led to a post-pandemic surge in the number of dogs ending up in rescue centres. Part of the reason for this was an incompatibility between the dog chosen and the owner’s lifestyle, and this mismatch is also something DogQuest is trying to tackle.

“People are choosing dogs that simply aren’t suitable for their lives,” Moore says. “For example, someone falls in love with a Bernese mountain dog puppy [large breed] without properly considering their home situation, lifestyle, exercise capacity, financial circumstances and how big the dog will get. So, we’ve set up a section on our website called Start Your Journey, which asks buyers about their lifestyle and helps match them to the breeds most likely to suit them.

“We’ve also built family trees into our listings so sellers can show the puppy’s mother, father and wider lineage, and the mother’s microchip can be recorded,” Moore adds. “Longer term, this gives us something incredibly important – traceability. If the same mother begins appearing across litters repeatedly or over consecutive breeding cycles, we can potentially identify a breeding pattern that deserves attention.”

Legislation to end Ireland’s reputation as ‘puppy farm capital of Europe’ advances

The founders have put a great deal of time and around €20,000 in hard cash into starting DogQuest with support from the Limerick local enterprise office, which provided the company with advice and a grow digital voucher, which supports small and medium enterprises to embrace digital technology.

“Setting up DogQuest was far more complicated than launching a traditional classified advertising website because of the different systems and verification layers we’ve built into our marketplace. Over approximately two years, we’ve gone through four developers trying to get the platform to exactly where we wanted it,” Moore says.

For now, DogQuest is focused on Ireland and is free to use for buyers, sellers and vets, and Moore says the founders are resigned to living with a no-revenue model until site traffic reaches a critical mass. Thereafter, the plan is to tap into a number of commercial opportunities and to start looking at other potential markets.

Brian Ivess is a barber by background, while Moore is an athlete and a secondary school PE teacher turned entrepreneur. Moore has two previous start-ups under his belt: an online geography revision platform for Leaving Cert students and Atlantik Body Care, which produces natural skincare products aimed at athletes and active individuals.

“DogQuest is not an anonymous marketplace,” Moore stresses. “Brian and I are putting our own names and faces behind the brand. People will see us on social media, hear from us, see us visiting vets and breeders and see us creating educational content around responsible puppy buying and ownership. We want transparency from the people using DogQuest, so we think we should offer exactly the same transparency ourselves. This is not the case with some other sites.

“The analogy I keep coming back to when describing what DogQuest does is that you wouldn’t buy a car simply because the seller has ticked a box saying it has an NCT. So, why should something as important as bringing a puppy into your family rely solely on the seller ticking a box to say it has been vaccinated and health checked?”

]]>Dara Mac Dónaill<![CDATA[Grand Theft Auto VI release could double New Zealand’s population on Thursday]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/grand-theft-auto-release-could-double-new-zealands-population-on-thursday/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/grand-theft-auto-release-could-double-new-zealands-population-on-thursday/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Companies around the world may notice a surprising surge in grave illness among their younger workers coinciding with the much-anticipated launch of Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI on Thursday morning.

The long wait since the fifth instalment in the series was released in 2013 could not come at a better time for a games development industry that has seen constrained budgets and lay-offs due to the impact of artificial intelligence.

The launch, however, could provide another unexpected boost as it becomes available to players as the clock strikes midnight in their region.

It leaves New Zealand bracing for a likely population explosion on Thursday morning as the staggered release times will mean the game is available there some 13 hours before the Irish launch, and 18 hours before New York. The staggered release times are to prevent the internet from breaking under the strain of gamers downloading GTA VI.

Online, console gamers in the northern hemisphere are busy strategising on how they can become Kiwis for the day.

Xbox users are changing their console’s region and using software – virtual private networks (VPNs) – to mask the country their internet connection is coming from.

Those on PlayStation are using VPNs to buy the New Zealand or Australia editions for the privilege of getting access half a day earlier.

The last game in the series sold nearly 235 million copies. Tens of millions, maybe hundreds of millions, of copies will be pre-sold (but not available to play) by the November 19th launch, meaning the 5.4 million-person island nation is set for a virtual population surge.

In Ireland, Inex, an internet exchange that accounts for two-thirds of Irish internet providers, saw record web traffic the day the game was made available to download (it won’t be available to play until the launch date in your region), with the average traffic on Tuesday 10th being more than 30 per cent higher than the previous record.

There was a time when budget day was the big digital traffic spinner – the craze around Fortnite changed that, Inex’s chief technology officer Nick Hilliard told Cantillon. Now it’s video games.

On Thursday morning, productivity may be down as generations of gamers will be staring out the window thinking of robbing banks, stealing cars and assaulting innocent pedestrians under the virtual Miami sun of GTA VI.

   <description>Die 31. Weltklimakonferenz (COP31) im türkischen Antalya geht auch dieses Jahr in die Verlängerung. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448767/">
   <title>Polen meldet Einschlag von Marschflugkörper</title>
   <description>Bei nächtlichen Angriffen auf die Ukraine ist polnischen Regierungsangaben zufolge ein russischer Marschflugkörper in den Luftraum Polens eingedrungen und abgestürzt. Zwei weitere Einschläge werden noch geprüft. Bei Nowy Lipowiec könne man bestätigen, dass es sich um einen Ch-101-Marschflugkörper handelt, zitierten polnische Medien am Freitag Verteidigungsminister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448765/">
   <title>Grüne feiern 40 Jahre im Parlament</title>
   <description>Mit einem Festakt im Parlament haben die Grünen am Freitag 40 Jahre im Parlament gefeiert. Die grüne Bundessprecherin Leonore Gewessler begrüßte Gründungsmitglieder und aktuelle Mitstreiterinnen und Mitstreiter mit „großem Respekt und unglaublichem Stolz“. Bundespräsident Alexander Van der Bellen, selbst elf Jahre lang Chef der Partei, sprach von der „Menschheitsaufgabe Klimanotstand“ und appellierte zur Kooperation.</description>

      <description>Die Vorschläge des Bundesrates für die Reform des Gesetzes zur Bankenstabilität stossen auf harsche Kritik. Der UBS fehlt die Verhältnismässigkeit, der Bankenverband hält sie für unausgewogen.</description>

A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm.

Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private.

InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w

— IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026

Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team.

 

“InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent.

They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another.

“InPost has built a leading position in Europe’s out-of-home delivery segment,” said FedEx’s CEO and president, Raj Subramaniam. “Connecting our global network…with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth.”

Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”.

President Macron has thanked Polish delivery giant InPost for its latest investment in France

The firm, which already operates over 9,000 parcel lockers in France through its subsidiary Mondial Relay, will now spend a further €500m to expand its presence https://t.co/caOGNQemfm

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026

InPost is the largest operator of parcel lockers in Europe, with around 70,000 across the continent. That includes roughly 30,000 in Poland and 16,000 in the UK, including in branches of the British Post Office, with over 23,000 more in the seven Eurozone countries where InPost operates.

In the second quarter of 2026, InPost had revenue of 4.18 billion zloty (€970 million), up 18.2% year on year, while its number of parcels handled rose 16% to 380.9 million.

The strongest revenue growth came in the eurozone, where sales increased 37.9%, followed by Poland, with 12.7% growth. Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose 9.8%.

Poland recently managed to prevent a planned Russian “false-flag operation” at the border that, if it had not been stopped, could have “ended tragically”, says a retired general who acts as an advisor to the defence minister.

His statement follows a report earlier this week by a leading newspaper, based on statements by unnamed senior officials, that Poland had foiled an attempt by Russia to carry out a major “provocation” on the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Polish government figures, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, have confirmed that a Russian operation at the border was prevented, though they have not provided further details.

Generał Mieczysław Bieniek o próbie rosyjskiej prowokacji przy granicy z Polską !!!

Polskie władze potwierdzają udaremnioną próbę rosyjskiej prowokacji przy granicy z obwodem królewieckim. – Udało się udaremnić, być może tragiczny w skutkach, incydent – przyznał w "Faktach po… pic.twitter.com/raQMfJ4uUp

— Andrzej Mitura #Mocnytakżeosobno (@AndrzejekMitura) November 19, 2026

“The public isn’t informed about everything,” retired general Mieczysław Bieniek, who acts as an advisor to defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday.

Bieniek then revealed that, “based on information we received from both our allies and our own intelligence services, we managed to thwart an incident with potentially tragic consequences, because the planned false-flag operation could have ended tragically”.

“For example, if a group of people crossed the border and later dressed in uniforms, whether Ukrainian or Polish, but were Russian citizens disguised as others, and carried out an attack on their target, the side whose uniforms were worn would naturally be blamed,” continued the general.

“Fortunately, nothing of the sort happened,” he added. “Certainly this preventative action [by Poland] forced the other side to desist from these acts.”

 

Bieniek’s comments followed a report published on Wednesday by the Rzeczpospolita daily, which said it had learned of a planned Russian sabotage operation on the border between Poland and the Kaliningrad exclave.

The newspaper, citing unnamed high-ranking figures from the uniformed services, said that the planned incident could have involved Russia mounting an attack on one of its own facilities but blaming it on Ukraine. Such actions are known as false-flag operations.

“It was supposed to be reminiscent of the Gleiwitz incident,” said one unnamed source, referring to a false-flag attack in 1939 staged by Nazi Germany, in which German operatives dressed in Polish uniforms. It was one of a number of such staged incidents used to justify the invasion of Poland.

🔴 Operacja polskich służb oraz wojska na przełomie października i listopada zapobiegła rosyjskiej prowokacji na granicy z obwodem królewieckim – wynika z ustaleń @marek_kozubal https://t.co/EFWsdlZUHY

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 18, 2026

According to Rzeczpospolita, concerns over this planned Russian operation were what prompted Poland to bolster security in regions along the Kaliningrad border in late October.

On 3 November, Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that Poland had “managed to prevent a provocation” on the border after “individuals with flashlights” were spotted. However, he did not provide further details at the time.

When Rzeczpospolita this week asked Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, if Russia had been planning a terrorist attack, he replied: “You’d have to ask the Russians. And they usually don’t admit to planning such actions. Even if we have such information, we don’t share it.”

“If we took certain steps, it was because we recognised there was a real threat,” added Siemoniak. “Appropriate actions were taken by the border guard, the police and the military. I can’t go into details.”

Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk claims that "individuals with flashlights" were observed at the Russian border last night.

"We very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and resources there, and managed to prevent a provocation," he added https://t.co/kD5OmpNagf

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026

On Wednesday afternoon, Kosiniak-Kamysz himself was asked about reports of a planned border provocation. “It didn’t happen, because we responded appropriately,” said the defence minister.

“Russia is rapidly climbing the escalation ladder, moving from airspace violations, attempted train bombings, sabotage of arms factories, as well as cyberspace activity, [and] it can also provoke at the border,” he continued, referring to some of the actions Russia has already taken against Poland.

However, Kosiniak-Kamysz did not comment on or provide any specific details of what kind of incident Poland may have prevented on the Kaliningrad border.

Later on Wednesday, Tusk himself reiterated to journalists that “we received signals that some unacceptable events could occur near the Polish-Russian border” and that “it seems that the mobilisation of the border guard and police in this place blocked any plans or ideas to carry out any provocation”.

However, he added that further details are “kept confidential for obvious reasons”.

Two Russian missiles and what is likely to have been a jet-powered drone struck Poland last night during large-scale attacks on Ukraine, the defence minister has confirmed https://t.co/QM2t2hOwlg

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2026

Poland’s government has for months been warning that Russia is planning escalatory provocations against eastern NATO states, which could involve border and airspace violations.

In June, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski even announced that he was “expecting an attack on Russian territory under a false flag, to which Putin will ‘respond'”. Sikorski pointed to the Gleiwitz incident as an example of such an operation.

On Friday morning, two Russian missiles and what is believed to be a drone entered Polish airspace and hit the ground in three locations. Tusk condemned the incident as a further “Russian escalation” and said that it was likely to have been “an intentional provocation”.

Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań.

Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities.

Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026

In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026

Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments.

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”.

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.
