]]>

Narwal has designed robots that can both vacuum and mop. Source: Narwal

Robots have entered homes, but the path to consumer adoption has been long and winding. iRobot Corp. was the pioneer but entered bankruptcy proceedings late in 2025. Narwal Robotics Corp. has spent a decade on research and development, testing 30 technical routes to self-cleaning robotic mops, and building a supply chain to retain cost control.

While iRobot has emerged from bankruptcy with a new owner, Narwal is working toward an initial public offering (IPO). The company, which has offices in Shenzhen, China, and Covina, Calif., is looking to embodied intelligence to take home robots from the “iPod stage” to the “iPhone moment,” according to founder and CEO Junbin Zhang.

Zhang and Icey Bin, head of global brand at Narwal, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report:

Narwal took time to understand the household space

Why has the household robotics market been so difficult to break into?

The household robotics market has exceptionally high barriers to entry in R&D, supply chain, and algorithm development. In the early days, there were no mature industry solutions to reference. For instance, Narwal spent three years with zero revenue solely focused on R&D, iterating the self-cleaning mop structure over 10 times from scratch.

Additionally, contract manufacturers were initially reluctant to cooperate due to the complex product structures and low initial volumes. On the software side, features like automatic mop washing require extremely precise positioning algorithms for the robot to frequently return to its base station, which the industry lacked at the time.

Most importantly, to achieve a high market penetration, a company must refine the product’s experience, quality, and cost to the reliable standards of mature home appliances, which is an incredibly difficult ceiling to break through.

iRobot struggled for a number of reasons. Haven’t other vacuum providers such as Dyson picked up market share?

Over the past decade, the core dimension of industry competition has fundamentally shifted from stacking hardware parameters to delivering a low-intervention, automated cleaning experience. While traditional handheld vacuums still have a place, overseas households face complex pain points that require automated solutions—such as deep cleaning for carpets and managing pet hair.

To address this, Narwal innovated a dedicated carpet deep-cleaning module that automatically lifts the mop and increases suction, boosting carpet cleaning performance by 40% to 50% compared to traditional models.

Furthermore, we pioneered the DualFlow tangle-free system to fundamentally solve the pet hair tangling issue. This paradigm shift toward comprehensive automation and solving highly specific pain points is why Chinese challengers have reshaped the global market landscape.

Submit your innovation now!

Technology and supply chain were built from scratch

How is Narwal’s technology and business model different from those of existing cleaning robot players?

Narwal stands out from incumbent players by rejecting the industry playbook of parameter stacking and scale-first growth, instead building original, user value-centered innovations across four core dimensions:

  1. Technology route: category-defining innovation from scratch: Instead of incremental upgrades to basic sweeping functions, Narwal created the entire self-cleaning robot mop category from its first product. Its proprietary technology portfolio — including self-developed SLAM algorithms, NarMind autonomous system, FlowWash hot water cleaning, and DualFlow tangle-free system — all target universal industry pain points rather than meaningless parameter competition.
  2. A model with full end-to-end control of the supply chain: Unlike the prevalent asset-light, OEM-heavy model, Narwal leverages the mature Greater Bay Area, a leading comprehensive manufacturing hub in southern China. Its full “Shenzhen R&D + Dongguan manufacturing” setup covers the full product lifecycle from development and design to manufacturing and delivery, enabling faster product iteration and consistent quality control.
  3. Operating logic: refined long-term management: Narwal rejects short-term tactics such as exchanging losses for market share and eroding brand value through price wars. It operates under a business-unit structure where R&D and frontline teams function as mutual profit centers, balancing innovation investment and market demand to avoid blind feature stacking or ineffective marketing spending.
  4. Strategic path: experience-first penetration: Contrary to the “chasing scale first, fixing experience later” industry norm, Narwal follows a long-term experience-first strategy: it polishes floor cleaning performance to mature home appliance standards first, then gradually reduces costs and drives market penetration through supply chain optimization, with the goal of turning robot vacuums from tech novelties into household essentials.

In what geographic regions have you found the most traction and why?

To date, Narwal’s products have entered more than 30 countries and regions globally, reaching over 6 million users. We have seen significant traction across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East.

Between January and April 2026, our overseas revenue grew by nearly 50% year-on-year. This success is primarily because we practice a “one country, one policy” approach, heavily customizing product features based on local lifestyle needs.

In North America, the U.S. is one of our most important markets. Our Flow 2 claimed the No. 1 spot in the robot vacuum new release category on Amazon U.S. within 24 hours of launch, with sales up 305% year over year versus the previous generation.

Key local optimizations include battery capacity and path planning upgrades for large single-family homes, plus a dedicated carpet deep-clean mode and DualFlow tangle-free system roller brush tailored to the high pet ownership rate. We have also established offline retail partnerships with major national chains including Best Buy and Costco.

In Europe, we have expanded steadily since 2024. During the 2025 Black Friday period, revenue in the French market surged 449% year on year, and first-launch sales across Europe grew 241% year on year.

Key local optimizations are enhanced carpet-cleaning performance and DualFlow tangle-free system for pet households, as well as water system adjustments for hard-water regions. We have a direct presence via our official website and Amazon in France, Italy, and Germany, with extended reach in Spain, Sweden, and the Netherlands, plus an extensive offline retail network.

Narwal address AI and privacy concerns

How do you see recent AI advances enabling more applications for consumer robots?

Recent AI advances are transforming consumer robots from executing “command-based cleaning” to performing “perception-based intelligent cleaning.” For example, Narwal pioneered the AI DirtSense technology and FlowWash hot water cleaning to sense floor dirt levels and automatically adjust cleaning power.

Furthermore, we were the first to mass-produce robot vacuums with dual-camera vision, allowing robots to achieve precise environment perception, obstacle avoidance, and scene recognition. Additionally, large language models enable natural language dialogue, allowing users to issue complex commands like “clean up the melon seeds near the sofa” instead of rigid keywords

When you mention “3D embodied intelligence,” how do you avoid the privacy concerns that affected iRobot?

Data privacy and security are core commitments across every market we operate in, and we have built multi-layer safeguards to address privacy risks. Beyond data governance, most of our products have obtained TÜV certification for product safety and quality as part of our broader commitment to being a trusted brand in people’s homes.

Minimized data collection by design: Our privacy policy explicitly states that Narwal does not automatically collect user photos or videos without user consent and affirmative user action. Sensitive network information, such as Wi-Fi passwords, is stored locally on the user’s robot and app only, and is never uploaded to our cloud servers.

Personal information collected is only used for necessary purposes, including providing product services, verifying accounts, optimizing product experience, ensuring security, and complying with legal obligations. We never repurpose it for unrelated uses.

Full regulatory compliance: Our products and services comply with applicable data protection laws and regulations in all operating markets, including GDPR in the EU/EEA and CPRA in California.

Cleaning robots are tailored for the U.S. market

How are you navigating tariffs and the recent  FCC restrictions? How do you ensure a reliable supply chain?

Regarding the FCC’s action, we want to assure our customers that Narwal’s current lineup is not impacted—every model sold in the U.S. today remains fully certified, fully supported, and available at retail. For future products, we are closely reviewing the FCC’s announcement, including the conditional approval process.

As for tariffs, we are currently evaluating what these new requirements would mean for our operations. To ensure a highly reliable supply chain, Narwal relies on an “end-to-end” closed-loop talent and manufacturing system based in the China Greater Bay Area. While overseas competitors might take months to prototype a product, our highly clustered supply chain lets us prototype and iterate within a week, giving us the efficiency to weather external shocks.

Are you customizing any features for the U.S. market?

Yes, we have customized products and operations for the U.S. market across product performance, scenario adaptation and compliance dimensions:

Cleaning scenario adaptation: For the high pet ownership rate in the U.S. market, we optimized the DualFlow tangle-free system roller brush to effectively solve the pet hair tangling pain point.

For the high carpet coverage rate, we launched a Carpet Deep Clean module. When the robot detects carpet, it automatically lifts the mop pad and increases negative pressure suction to enhance deep carpet cleaning performance, improving dust removal by 40–50% compared to standard models.

Home size and runtime adaptation: For the common scenario of large single-family homes in the U.S., we upgraded battery capacity and optimized path planning for large-area cleaning. Our “charge while washing” design allows the robot to charge while returning to the base station to wash the mop, extending effective runtime without increasing battery size and weight.

We also enhanced AI navigation powered by dual-camera vision to handle complex floor plans in open-concept homes and large villas.

Stain scenario adaptation: Our FlowWash hot water cleaning technology continuously cleans the mop with fresh hot water during cleaning, preventing secondary contamination from dirty mops. This is optimized for common U.S. household stain scenarios such as kitchen food spills, muddy paw prints, and water tracked in from pools.

Robot vacuums approach their ‘iPhone moment’

When you say “iPhone moment,” are you thinking of apps and a platform approach, increasing levels of autonomy, or something else?

The “iPhone moment” describes a maturity leap for the entire robot vacuum category, rather than an app ecosystem or platform business model.

Right now, robot vacuums are still in the “iPod stage”: they only address flat floor cleaning, and remain tech novelties for early adopters. Penetration in China stands below 10%, while roughly 15% in mature overseas markets — far below the 90%+ rate for mature home appliances like refrigerators and washing machines.

The category will hit the “iPhone moment” inflection point when product experience, reliability and cost all reach mature home appliance standards. At that point, robot vacuums will become a daily household necessity, and penetration will see explosive growth.

Alongside mass adoption, products will also evolve in parallel from flat floor-cleaning tools to full-space “housekeepers” with 3D cleaning and organizing capabilities — the embodied intelligence form we are working toward.

]]> Disseqt AI, a Dublin-based AI assurance platform, has raised €7.3 million ($8 million) to help enterprises deploy AI agents safely, at scale and enable them to meet regulatory requirements.

Gresham House Ventures led the round, with participation from Sure Valley Ventures (SVV), Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland, alongside angels including senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, and cricket legend Rahul Dravid.

Apoorva Kumar, CEO and co-founder of Disseqt AI, says, “Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. That gap is what stops AI from going live, and it is what we built Disseqt to close. We test before launch, control in real time and keep the audit trail, independently of the model providers.

“When your agent is talking to 80 million people, or processing thousands of banking transactions, ‘good enough’ isn’t an option. This funding lets us bring that standard to many more enterprises. AI governance and assurance needs to become a standard part of how every enterprise runs AI.”

Disseqt’s funding follows several European investment rounds in AI-agent assurance, governance and security during 2026.

In the UK, Geordie AI raised €25 million to strengthen AI-agent governance, Trent AI secured €11 million for agentic cybersecurity, and AI Score received €4.6 million to support safer enterprise AI adoption. Spain also recorded investments in NeuralTrust (€17.2 million) and AI evaluation platform Galtea (€2.7 million).

Closer to home, Irish-founded Evervault raised €21 million for adjacent encrypted-data infrastructure.

Together with rounds secured by Mindgard, Overmind and Hybridity, these announcements represent approximately €111.8 million in 2026 funding, excluding Disseqt’s investment.

Rohit Mathur, Partner, Gresham House Ventures, adds, “We see AI governance and assurance becoming essential infrastructure as enterprises put AI into live operations. Companies need to test and control their AI with tools that sit apart from the model providers they rely on. Disseqt does that across the full life of an AI application, and its early customers include some of the most demanding regulated buyers in Europe.

“Enterprise AI deployment spend scaled to £130 billion by September 2026, up from £25 billion last year, and this will accelerate many-folds in a short span. However it won’t happen without proper governance and assurance which is what Disseqt AI is built for.”

Disseqt was founded in late 2025 by Apoorva Kumar (CEO), Manish Atri (CTO) and Cyril Treacy (COO). Between them they have held senior roles at Microsoft, AWS and Salesforce across enterprise software, AI and cybersecurity.

According to the company, AI agents are moving from answering questions to doing real work, handling requests, accessing company data and taking actions inside business systems. McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 40% of respondents at companies with more than $1 billion in annual revenue were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, up from 27% a year earlier.

However, agents do not always behave as intended and can introduce risks even while pursuing assigned tasks. In October 2026, OpenAI disclosed two internal incidents in which coding agents weakened safety monitoring, with one falsely denying the change. As businesses give agents greater access to data, tools and customer interactions, ensuring they operate within company policy is becoming increasingly important.

This is where AI assurance comes in. It provides ongoing testing and monitoring to ensure AI systems behave as intended.

Disseqt enables enterprises to test applications and agents before launch, enforce company policies once live and monitor their behaviour continuously, blocking outputs that breach those policies while maintaining evidence for audit and oversight.

For example, enterprises can test whether an agent can be prompted to reveal confidential customer data, address vulnerabilities before deployment and retain a record of the results for audit.

The approach has already been applied at scale and across multiple customers. In a project for a global sports league’s fan engagement agent, used by 80 million fans, Disseqt reportedly improved the safe-response rate from 80% to 99% across tests covering safety, bias and privacy risks. Disseqt reports that no unsafe outputs were detected when the original failing tests were repeated following fixes. Similarly, Disseqt’s provide assurance for a large European Bank credit card services programme.

Kara Owen, British Ambassador to Ireland, says, “Huge congratulations to Apoorva and the Disseqt AI team on this fantastic milestone. It is great to see an innovative Irish AI company expanding its presence in the UK and tapping into the UK’s deep technology, investment and AI ecosystem. Their expansion into London is a great example of the opportunities for ambitious Irish tech companies to use the UK as a platform to scale, grow internationally and reach new markets. I’m delighted to see Disseqt AI strengthening the already vibrant technology links between Ireland and the UK.”

The funding will help Disseqt win more enterprise customers and expand internationally, as it works towards its goal of becoming the assurance layer enterprises rely on for every AI agent they deploy. The company is hiring across sales, operations and technology.

All existing investors, including QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures, participated in the round, alongside new investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, and leading European entrepreneurs Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee. This round brings the company’s total funding to more than $515 million. 

Hristo Borisov, co-founder and CEO of Payhawk, said, “The role of the finance team is rapidly moving away from manual checks, lengthy reconciliations and labour-intensive work towards becoming more strategic. While most companies use AI to speed up existing processes, we built AI agents to fundamentally rethink how finance operates.”

Founded in 2018 in Sofia by Hristo Borisov, Boyko Karadzhov, and Konstantin Dzhengozov, Payhawk is an AI-native spend management platform that orchestrates global money across Bills, Cards, Expenses, Travel, and Procurement for maximum control, automation and savings.

The company plans to move beyond spend management to build an operating system (OS) where AI agents, payments, and enterprise controls run finance together. 

“Through our technology, finance departments can benefit from ‘zero-touch finance’, where neither the finance professional nor the employee deals with any admin work. 77% of our customers use our agents daily across financial control, procurement, travel and reporting to save time and money for their businesses. But AI alone cannot deliver this transformation, it must be combined with a robust payment infrastructure and enterprise controls to truly unlock the potential of every enterprise in the new AI era,” added Borisov. 

According to the company, ERP systems, banks, procurement platforms, treasury products, travel tools and spend platforms are all becoming more intelligent with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. But Payhawk argues that making each application smarter does not automatically create a smarter finance operation.

“Integrations connect systems. MCP makes information easier to access. But an operating system changes how the entire finance function works. As software moves from recommending actions to actually taking them, that distinction becomes much more important,” stated Borisov. 

The company is building its finance OS around three interconnected layers: AI agents that perform financial work; payments infrastructure that lets agents safely interact with money; and enterprise controls that determine what agents can do and when human intervention is required. 

Borisov revealed that Payhawk aims to build a global finance category built from Europe. “Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else. We want to build the infrastructure through which businesses around the world run their financial operations in the age of AI. Being born in Europe has exposed us to this complexity from day one. We know what it takes for our customers to stay in control with their businesses spread around the world while scaling and while trying to be efficient at the same time. The window to define that category is open now — and we are moving fast,” he commented. 

Headquartered in London, Payhawk now operates across 33 countries and 12 offices, with a platform that spans multiple currencies, banking systems, payment rails, regulations and local practices. 

Payhawk reports it achieved positive cash flow in Q3 and still holds 70% of the capital it raised in its 2022 funding round. In March 2022, it raised an additional €89 million and extended its funding to €191 million, making it Bulgaria’s first unicorn. 

In November 2021, the company raised €99 million in Series B funding, valuing it at €505 million. It raised €16.5 million in Series A in April 2021 and €3 million in a Seed round in March 2020. 

The company notes that its business model relies on predictable subscription pricing rather than card interchange, aligning growth with helping customers save money rather than incentivising them to spend more. In the US, for example, its Financial Controller Agent works with customers’ existing business cards, eliminating the need to switch providers or reissue cards.

]]> Europe’s tech ecosystem is heading for its second-best investment year on record, with bigger funding rounds, a new generation of founders and startups scaling at unprecedented speed.

But the continent’s structural weaknesses remain: venture capital is increasingly concentrated, the US is pulling ahead in AI investment, and European companies still struggle to access growth capital.

Published today, Atomico’s State of European Tech 2026 report, titled Build it. Scale it. Own it., offers a data-driven look at the continent’s progress and the obstacles holding it back. Here are five findings that stand out.

“The data on the European tech ecosystem stopped being ambiguous some time ago. We have built a world-class tech ecosystem; we just don’t let ourselves believe it. The value still to come from European tech is bigger than
everything it has created so far. Nothing is missing – the capital, talent and demand are all here, but they’re locked or misallocated. Our founders are flying into the wind. It still works, but it doesn’t let you reach top speed,” says Tom Wehmeier, State of European Tech report founder, Partner at Atomico.

1. European tech investment is bouncing back, up 62% to €73 billion

European startups are on track to attract €73 billion ($81 billion) in 2026, a 62% increase from the €45 billion ($50 billion) invested in 2025. That would make this the second-strongest year on record, behind the €85 billion ($94 billion) reached in 2021.

After three years of investment hovering between €36 billion ($40 billion) and €45 billion ($50 billion), the recovery marks a clear turning point. Median European Seed rounds have grown 27% year-on-year, while Series A rounds are up 30%.

The surge is being driven partly by AI companies and larger funding rounds. Among the standout deals are UK-based Wayve’s €1 billion Series D to scale AI-powered autonomous driving, German DefenceTech startup Quantum Systems’ €1 billion Series D, and British AI voice company ElevenLabs’ €424 million Series D.

However, the €73 billion figure remains a full-year projection based on data through 30 September 2026, rather than a final tally.

2. Billion-dollar rounds are booming, but capital is concentrating

Europe recorded 13 funding rounds worth at least $1 billion during the first nine months of 2026, raising a combined €20 billion ($22 billion). These deals accounted for 37% of all capital invested during the period.

For comparison, only 15 rounds of that size took place between 2017 and 2025 combined.

Standout examples include Mistral AI’s €3 billion Series D and Nscale’s €1.7 billion Series C.

The trend is reaching the earliest stages, too. Paris-based AMI raised €890 million in Seed funding.

This points to the fact that Europe can now finance enormous technology ambitions, but a disproportionately large share of investment is reaching a handful of companies.

3. Europe is producing more founders than the US, but fewer are getting funded

An estimated 40,000 people started technology companies in Europe in 2026, up 36% from 2025 and 80% from 2024.

Europe now accounts for 29% of the world’s new tech founders, narrowly ahead of the US at 28%, although Atomico cautions that Chinese entrepreneurship may be underrepresented in its dataset.

AI is helping lower the barrier to launching businesses, with more than 60% of founders now starting companies alone.

Yet there is a catch. The number of European startups securing their first funding round declined 28% between 2021 and 2025, with further decreases projected for 2026.

Europe’s entrepreneurial pipeline is expanding faster than its early-stage funding opportunities. More startups are being created, but fewer are getting their first institutional cheque.

4. Europe’s AI boom is impressive, until you compare it with America

Europe’s AI investment is accelerating, but the gap with the US is staggering.

During the first nine months of 2026, approximately €18 billion ($20 billion) flowed into European AI and compute companies, compared with €258 billion ($284 billion) in the United States.

That means the US invested more than 14 times as much as Europe in these technologies over the same period.

The infrastructure gap is similarly significant, with Europe accounting for only around 7% of global AI computing capacity, compared with roughly 72% in the US.

European startups such as Mistral AI and AMI demonstrate the continent’s technical capabilities, but competing in frontier AI requires more than talented researchers. It demands enormous computing resources and long-term capital.

The risk is that Europe develops world-class AI innovations while remaining dependent on infrastructure and financing controlled elsewhere.

5. Europe can build global champions, but scaling remains its Achilles’ heel

Europe’s technology ecosystem is now worth €4 trillion ($4.4 trillion), up from €829 billion ($900 billion) in 2017. During the first nine months of 2026, another 58 European companies reached billion-dollar valuations, compared with 42 throughout 2025.

Stockholm-based Lovable illustrates how quickly European companies can grow. The AI startup reached €91 million ($100 million) in ARR just eight months after reporting its first €911k ($1 million), and subsequently secured a €343 million Series C.

Yet the structural funding gap persists. European startups take a median of 29 months to progress from Series A to Series B, compared with 20 months in the US.

Meanwhile, European pension funds allocate just 0.006% of their assets to venture capital, compared with 0.028% in the US.

Atomico’s message is clear

Europe no longer needs to prove it can create ambitious startups. Its next challenge is mobilising enough capital, improving conditions for scaling and ensuring that more of the value generated by European technology stays in Europe.

]]> MountAIn, a Grenoble-based frugal AI infrastructure company, has raised €7.3 million in Seed funding to run advanced AI on microcontrollers costing less than €9.11 ($10). 

The round was led by 360 Capital and Supernova Invest, with participation from Crédit Agricole Alpes Développement (C2AD) and additional support from Bpifrance.

“The next great leap in AI won’t happen only in data centres. It will happen mostly across the billions of devices operating in the physical world. That requires embedded AI that is both energy-efficient and affordable. MountAIn delivers exactly that, with a level of performance we haven’t seen anywhere else,” said François Tison, Partner at 360 Capital.

MountAIn was founded in 2025 by Vincent Huard, Olivier Montfort, and David Nahmani with a goal of making AI accessible on ultra-low-cost microcontrollers. The founders argue that the vast majority of the world’s physical equipment runs on microcontrollers that consume milliwatts of power, yet AI development tools are built primarily for GPUs.

With its MountainCore platform, the company addresses this mismatch by automatically adapting complete computer vision applications, the AI model, pre-processing, post-processing, and data movement, to run within the strict memory, compute, and power limits of low-cost embedded processors.

“AI models are designed for GPUs and data centres, yet most equipment in the real world could run on microcontrollers consuming just milliwatts of power,” said Huard, CEO and co-founder of MountAIn.

According to the company, MountainCore can reduce model memory requirements by up to threefold, improve use of on-chip AI accelerators and preserve model accuracy without retraining. It also compresses deployment timelines that previously stretched across months into a matter of hours.

MountAIn has built partnerships with Teledyne e2v, chip designer Alif Semiconductor, and computer vision platform Roboflow, which serves more than two million developers and 80,000 companies. Its IBEX autonomous vision sensor, which runs on solar power, connects via satellite and consumes under 100 milliwatts, is designed for use cases such as early wildfire detection and infrastructure monitoring without relying on constant cloud connectivity.

The company also runs an invite-only Early Adopter Program (EAP), which gives select engineering teams a structured path to test MountainCore against a defined model, hardware target and success condition, allowing participants to help with product development using evidence from real deployments.

“The AI model is only part of the equation. MountainCore enables the entire application to run on these tiny processors. What once took months of engineering now takes hours, and major industrial companies such as Teledyne are already putting the technology to work. This financing will help us turn that early success into large-scale commercial deployment,” added Huard.

The funding comes at a time when demand for on-device AI is growing sharply across industrial, infrastructure and remote monitoring sectors. While the demand is there, the tools remain optimised for data-centre-grade hardware, which is impractical at the edge, and MountAIn plans to use the new capital to close this gap.

MountAIn says it will use the new funding to accelerate MountainCore’s commercial rollout, expand its engineering team in Grenoble and strengthen the company’s footprint in both Europe and Silicon Valley. It is set to demonstrate MountainCore’s industrial capabilities at CES in January 2027, with target customers including semiconductor manufacturers, smart camera makers and industrial equipment companies.

Agarwal, an NYU School of Law graduate, built a venture capital law firm from scratch to 75 deals and a top-tier Legal 500 ranking within three years.

With Perry AI, they are building and maintaining a live legal memory for private capital markets, one capable of capturing every right, obligation, side letter commitment, and negotiated position a fund has made, across every deal. AI agents then act on that record, reviewing documents, flagging issues, preparing drafts, and coordinating in-house teams with external counsel through one shared, live workspace.

The platform covers the full fund lifecycle, from fund formation and capital deployment to portfolio and fund management, and exit. It serves both fund teams and the law firms advising them. Perry AI says law firms can also white-label the platform under their own brand, keeping clients engaged for the life of a fund rather than only during live transactions.

“I spent more than 15 years advising funds, and every deal had the same undercurrent: a scramble against the clock, in a high-stakes, regulated world, with the constant fear that something had been missed. A side letter promise, a consent or preemption right, an MFN obligation buried three deals back. Generic AI can’t take that fear away, because it doesn’t know the fund. Perry AI does,” said Patel, co-founder and CEO of Perry AI.

He added, “It remembers every position a fund has taken and acts on it, so legal teams can move fast and still sleep at night. Demand has been exceptional, and this round lets us build on our momentum in Europe and take Perry AI across the US and Asia.”

The company says funds already using Perry AI manage over €1.4 billion ($1.5 billion) in assets under management across more than 1,000 portfolio companies. Its users report working 90% faster, with deal signing times on live transactions reduced from 84 days to just 13 days,

The fresh capital will accelerate Perry AI’s expansion into the United States and Asia, while deepening its European and UK growth. The company also plans to extend the platform beyond deal execution into areas such as fund formation, secondaries, fund transfers, LP reporting, MFN tracking, and co-invest allocation, several of which are already live.

]]> Europe’s ambitions for AI sovereignty depend on giving its startups the resources to succeed, innovate and compete with established companies. As it stands, the EU remains heavily reliant on digital technologies developed and managed from elsewhere, raising questions about its ability to control the systems underpinning its economy.  

In June this year, the European Commission unveiled its European Technological Sovereignty Package. This includes the Cloud and AI Development Act, which specifically aims to support the research, development and innovation of next-generation AI technologies, including frontier AI models.  

The Tech Sovereignty Package also aims to fast-track the implementation of the European Commission’s existing AI Continent Action Plan. This encompasses many areas that are central to the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions, including physical infrastructure, talent development, and regulatory simplification. One of the most notable of these is access to large volumes of high-quality data, which the plan specifically highlights as a requirement for bolstering AI innovation. 

For European AI startups, publicly available web data is a valuable resource for training models and building services that rely on current information. Yet emerging licensing models that treat public data as exclusive, regulatory uncertainties and restrictions on automated access risk putting that resource beyond the reach of smaller developers. Maintaining responsible access to the open web is therefore central to enabling businesses of all sizes to contribute to the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions.  

AI sovereignty depends on an open web 

The internet itself was built on the principle that information can be published and accessed widely, without any one company controlling access to it. Within a few years of launching the World Wide Web, CERN placed the software in the public domain for anyone to use, modify and distribute. This openness allowed businesses, researchers and developers to build on shared foundations without seeking permission from a single technology provider.  

This principle underpinned, and continues to support, both the development and functioning of frontier AI systems. Varied public web data can help reduce gaps and biases in training data, helping AI models to deliver accurate, unbiased outputs. The rise of agentic AI has further increased the importance of access to public web data. It is being deployed across a growing range of services, from personal shopping and travel assistants to business research and IT support. 

Microsoft’s Work Trend annual index report found a 15-fold increase in active agents across its Microsoft 365 ecosystem between March 2025 and March 2026. For agents carrying out tasks on the web, however, restrictions on access to current information can limit their effectiveness. For example, an agent comparing suppliers or booking travel needs to check changing prices, availability and terms before acting. 

In October, research found that roughly a third of the several hundred leading US commerce, travel and reservation websites it tested blocked Meta’s Muse agent, while another third challenged or restricted its access. The biggest problem here is not for Meta, who have been negotiating leverage and large financial resources for legal disputes, but many smaller agent developers do not.

This limits their ability to innovate, as their agents have less access to up-to-date information. Consumers also lose out, with fewer competing services to choose from and agents that may be unable to compare the full range of products, prices and offers available. 

Such arbitrary restrictions threaten the EU’s AI ambitions as its AI startups are excluded from the market by the decisions of competing private companies. They also raise questions about consumer sovereignty in the free market and how it may be limited. 

While regulators discuss opt-outs, blanket blocks are implemented 

In September 2026, the European Commission launched a consultation on whether the EU’s copyright framework needs additional measures, including those addressing the use of copyright-protected content in AI. The resulting policy decisions could have significant implications far beyond AI.  

A key risk is that overly broad measures have unintended consequences as data resources previously used for innovation and value creation become virtually useless for society. They become exclusive to the biggest market players. For European startups, this translates directly into a competitive disadvantage against companies operating under more proportionate regulatory regimes. 

While the EU is still considering the scope of copyright holders’ opt-outs and how they should work, private companies are already implementing their own mechanisms, waiting neither for regulation nor for the website owner to actually make the choice. ​​If web hosts and platforms get to make such decisions instead of the users that created the content or the websites that published it, copyright will slowly lose its meaning.  

This will not be because of AI companies accessing content but because of the lack of control publishers will have over who can access their content. Both AI companies and publishers are seeking clarity over who can access content, for what purposes and on whose terms. These questions should be resolved through clear rules that give rights holders meaningful control, preserve lawful access to public web data and hold those who misuse it accountable. 

The web must remain open. This means lawful information published openly on the web should remain accessible. Personal, private information should remain protected, while the collection and use of personal data must comply with data-protection laws. And this is where the issue lies. We need to clearly distinguish what information is public and what information is deemed private.  

Beyond these regulatory questions, the risk for EU startups is the creation of a pay-to-play economy that favours large technology companies and well-financed incumbents with negotiated access to public data. This raises the cost of innovation and restricts European startups’ ability to catch up and compete, undermining the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions. 

Enabling the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions 

Creating a commercial and regulatory environment that supports innovation and global competitiveness is central to developing the EU’s sovereign AI ecosystem. Existing regulations and ongoing policy initiatives such as the AI Act provide an important foundation, but further work is needed to clarify compliance requirements and address barriers that favour well-financed incumbents.  

Access to the same publicly available information should not depend solely on a company’s financial resources or its ability to negotiate preferential deals. The EU needs to balance legitimate access to public web data with the protection of copyright and platforms’ commercial interests. These objectives can coexist, but developers and publishers need clearer rules about what information can be collected, for which purposes and under what conditions. 

Ultimately, the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions depend not only on investment in infrastructure and talent but also on European companies’ ability to access and use diverse, up-to-date data.

Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas.

The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.

The post Aer Lingus unveils all-new A330 cabins, including its first Premium Economy cabin appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Irish flag carrier will roll out the transformation across 10 Airbus A330 aircraft from next year, with new Business Class suites, a new Premium Economy cabin and a redesigned Economy cabin.

Aer Lingus unveiled its all-new in-flight experience on 18 November, showcasing the major transformation for transatlantic flights on its Airbus A330 fleet. The project introduces the airline’s first-ever Premium Economy cabin, alongside reimagined Business Class and Economy products.  

When will Aer Lingus’ new cabins enter service?

The first refurbished aircraft will take to the skies on 1 October, 2027, initially on select Dublin-New York (JFK) flights. More North America routes will follow as further aircraft refurbishments are completed.

The nose-to-tail transformation of 10 A330s represents one of the carrier’s most significant investments in the onboard passenger experience. Alongside the three redesigned cabins, it brings new seating, dining and inflight technology.

Why the Irish carrier’s transformation matters

The upgrade comes as Aer Lingus faces tough trading conditions. The airline’s profits have fallen 57% as fuel prices surged. It is cutting capacity by 6% and dropping underperforming routes.

The refurbishment, and particularly the introduction of a Premium Economy cabin, is essential for the airline to stay competitive on the transatlantic market. The overhaul also modernises ageing A330 interiors, with the airline investing in higher-yielding seats, while trimming costs elsewhere.

Aer Lingus eyes up to 500 job cuts as it works to trim costs Aer Lingus eyes up to 500 job cuts as it works to trim costs

Inspired by Ireland

Aer Lingus’ distinctive Irish identity runs through the new interiors. The colours, materials and design draw on Ireland’s lush landscapes, coastlines and cultural heritage. Botany Weaving, in Dublin’s Liberties, has developed bespoke, locally sourced fabrics with subtle Ogham-inspired details.

Lynne Embleton, CEO, Aer Lingus described the ambition of the redesigned cabin interior as “simple.” It’s about giving customers “greater choice, comfort and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus,” she continued.

“This investment is much more than the introduction of a new cabin,” she said. “It is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy and, for the first time in Aer Lingus’ history, introducing Premium Economy.”

What passengers can expect from Aer Lingus’ Premium Economy

The introduction of Premium Economy marks a milestone for the Irish carrier, providing passengers with more choice on Atlantic crossings. The dedicated four-row cabin features 28 next-generation Recaro R4 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. Every seat has an integrated footrest and privacy-enhancing seat wings, with a 380-inch pitch, 18-19 inches of width, and a 9-inch recline.

Customers will be served a three-course meal and complimentary drinks throughout the flight. They will also receive bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones.

Aer Lingus means business

The Business Class cabin has 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 layout, meaning every passenger will have direct aisle access and a private suite with a closing door. Each seat converts into a fully flat bed, expanding to 78 inches in length.

The Business Class menu focuses on seasonal Irish ingredients combined with contemporary cuisine inspired by the airline’s transatlantic network. Passengers can also help themselves to snacks and refreshments from a self-service bar.

Elevated economy experience

Economy passengers also benefit from the refurbishment, with new ergonomic seating that offers greater comfort and personal space. The dining menu has also been refreshed and a new self-service snack bar is available.

How next-generation technology will transform the passenger experience

Every refurbished A330 aircraft will have Panasonic Astrova in-flight entertainment, with larger 4K HD screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity and USB-C charging. Meanwhile, customised mood lighting is designed to reduce the effects of jet lag and create a more relaxed onboard environment.

Free, ultrafast WiFi connectivity, already available across all Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes, ensures passengers stay as connected at 30,000 feet as they are on the ground.

The reveal follows Aer Lingus’ recent launch of ‘The Irish Airline’, a North American brand campaign aimed at introducing Aer Lingus to a wider US audience.

“As our new ‘The Irish Airline’ campaign builds awareness of Aer Lingus in North America, our new cabins bring our distinctive Irish identity to the onboard experience,” concluded Embleton.

The post Russia’s rare An-72P border patrol aircraft spotted in new exercise footage appeared first on AGN.

]]> Fresh footage published on Russian social media appears to show one of the country’s rare An-72P armed patrol aircraft taking part in a live-fire exercise.

The specialised variant, developed for the Soviet KGB’s border troops and now operated by the FSB’s Border Service Aviation branch, has rarely been seen in recent years, prompting speculation that the type is returning to more active use.

Rare An-72P patrol aircraft appears to return to FSB service

On 18 November, the Russian Telegram Channel, Fighter-Bomber posted a video of an Antonov An-72P patrol aircraft in flight carrying out live-fire exercises. The family is distinctive due to its high-mounted Lotarev D-36 Turbofans.

According to reporting by Ukraine’s Militarnyi news outlet, it appears that the rare An-72P patrol aircraft has been restored to service with the Russian Border Service Aviation of the Federal Security Service (FSB).

One documented 2001 incident involved an An-72P firing on a fishing vessel (“Albatros-101”) after it refused to stop.

Reprising its old KGB role

Nicknamed Cheburashka, the An-72P is a specialized patrol variant of the Soviet-era An-72 military transport aircraft, developed by Antonov.

It was developed at the request of the Soviet Union’s KGB border troops to patrol maritime borders and intercept vessels caught violating territorial waters. Historically, it was particularly noted for operations around the disputed Kuril Islands.

Militarnyi writes, “Unlike the standard transport variant, the An-72P, which made its maiden flight in 1984, was equipped with weapons for engaging surface and ground targets. In particular, the aircraft can carry a UPK-23-250 gun pod fitted with a twin-barrel 23 mm GSh-23L cannon.”

In temporarily occupied Crimea, @usf_army operators, jointly with @DI_Ukraine, hit an Orion UAV depot (4 drones destroyed), an An-72P patrol aircraft, and a P-37 radar. https://t.co/WRrgPmOrSi

— Defense of Ukraine (@DefenceU) April 2, 2026

In addition, it carries two underwing pylons able to carry UB-32M pods loaded with 64 S-5 unguided aircraft rockets as well as 100 kg aerial bombs. Other capabilities include limited troop/paratroop transport, life rafts/buoys, and STOL performance for remote areas.

Ukraine has claimed to have destroyed one An-72P in Crimea. Some claim the airframe was an old, abandoned ex-Ukrainian example parked at the base.

So far, two An-12s, one An-22, and eight An-26s appear in Oryx’s visually confirmed data.

Dutch F-35As intercept three Russian aircraft during Baltic Air Policing scramble Dutch F-35As intercept three Russian aircraft during Baltic Air Policing scramble

Russia’s fleet of Antonov An-12, An-26, An-72-series aircraft

AGN has previously reported on a Dallas Analytics analysis that suggests Russia is having major issues maintaining its legacy An-series fleet, for which it has no replacement.

Reporting on leaked Russian documents, Dallas Analytics wrote, “Russia currently operates approximately 368 An-series aircraft (An-12, An-26, An-72) belonging to the Ministry of Defence, the National Guard, and the FSB Aviation branch, of which 143 require repairs.”

The documents carried warnings that without urgent measures, the fleet would be forced out of service. Without Ukrainian Antonov support and expertise to help maintain the aircraft, the fleet is becoming increasingly unserviceable.

On 17 November 2026, a Russian Air Force Antonov An-12 transport aircraft crashed near Yagunovo, Kemerovo Oblast, Russia. At least 17 people on board died. Representative photo of An-12BK, 15 red. https://t.co/ltE1Yb5Xy2

Still, it remains unclear how dire it is for the entire fleet. Instead of a complete retirement, it may be more reasonable to see an increasing share of the fleet cannibalized to keep an ever-shrinking share of the fleet operational.

Separately, earlier this week, a Russian Air Force An-12 cargo aircraft reportedly crashed in Kemerovo, Siberia, killing all 17 occupants.

]]> Bell completes first MV-75 fuselage as US Army’s next-gen tiltrotor takes shape https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/bell-completes-first-fuselage-us-army-mv-75-cheyenne-ii/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:31:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57432 Bell Textron has completed the first fuselage of the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II tiltrotor at its Wichita facility, advancing the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft programme toward structural testing and first flight.

The post Bell completes first MV-75 fuselage as US Army’s next-gen tiltrotor takes shape appeared first on AGN.

]]> Bell Textron has completed the first fuselage of the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II, bringing the next-generation tiltrotor a step closer to flight testing.

Designed to fly twice as fast and twice as far as existing Army helicopters, the aircraft is being developed to carry troops and supplies over much greater distances.

The fuselage was built at Bell’s Wichita Assembly Center in Kansas and has been delivered to its Amarillo facility in Texas, where it will be joined with the aircraft’s completed wing structure and engine nacelles.

The milestone, announced on 16 November, comes two years after Bell selected Wichita as the manufacturing centre for the fuselage of the MV-75, which is being developed under the US Army’s Future Long Range Assault Aircraft (FLRAA) programme.

The aircraft is intended to transform how the Army moves troops, equipment and supplies across large distances, particularly in areas where conventional helicopters face limitations in speed and range.

Bell said the fuselage was assembled in four major sections covering the forward, middle and rear portions of the aircraft, followed by the joining of the structures and installation of the outer skins.

The Wichita facility uses advanced drilling and manufacturing equipment intended to shorten production times while maintaining structural accuracy.

“This achievement is a testament to the dedication and agility of Bell and the entire MV-75 team, who rapidly established infrastructure and moved with purpose to design and assemble the first fuselage,” said Adam Blackford, general manager of Bell’s Wichita Assembly Center.

“The completion of this fuselage reflects our unwavering commitment to delivering the MV-75 Cheyenne to our warfighters,” Blackford said.

What happens next?

The completed fuselage will be joined with the wings and nacelles at Amarillo before being placed in a purpose-built structural test fixture.

Bell will use the fixture to calibrate strain gauges and apply controlled loads to the aircraft’s structure. These tests are intended to establish whether the airframe can withstand the forces it will encounter during operation. The work is an essential step before flight testing begins.

Other parts of the aircraft have also been progressing through manufacturing and testing. In October, Bell announced that the first nacelle structures had been completed and successfully fitted to the wings.

The company also began testing the MV-75’s gearboxes at its Drive System Test Lab in Grand Prairie, Texas.
The gearboxes form part of the aircraft’s drive system and support electrical generators, hydraulic pumps and cooling equipment for the engines and nacelles.

Meanwhile, Bell is testing flight-control computers, electronic components, displays and other systems at its Weapon System Integration Lab in Arlington, Texas.

These ground tests allow engineers to identify problems with the aircraft’s software and electronic systems before they are installed in a flying prototype.

Why the US Army wants the MV-75

The MV-75 is being developed to address a longstanding limitation of military helicopters as their ability to take off and land vertically comes at the expense of speed and long-distance performance.

The US Army’s UH-60 Black Hawk has served as the backbone of its assault and utility helicopter fleet for decades. It carries troops, transports supplies, evacuates casualties and supports a wide range of military operations.

The MV-75 is designed to perform many of those missions over substantially greater distances.

Unlike a conventional helicopter, the MV-75 uses a tiltrotor configuration, with large propellers mounted at the ends of its wings.

During take-off and landing, the propellers face upwards, allowing the aircraft to operate much like a helicopter.

Once airborne, they tilt forwards, enabling the aircraft to fly like a fixed-wing aeroplane.

This arrangement allows it to combine vertical take-off capability with the higher cruising speeds and longer range associated with conventional aircraft.

Bell says the MV-75 will offer more than twice the speed and range of existing Army rotorcraft.

The aircraft is derived from Bell’s V-280 Valor demonstrator, which was developed to prove the tiltrotor concept for future military operations.

The V-280 was designed around a cruising speed of approximately 280 knots, significantly faster than the Black Hawk.

The Army has also cited a range of approximately 2,440 nautical miles for the MV-75. The greater range is intended to allow military units to operate from bases farther away from hostile forces, reducing their dependence on forward airfields and refuelling points.

It could also enable commanders to move troops rapidly between widely separated locations without relying on the same number of intermediate stops required by conventional helicopters.

How the MV-75 differs from the Osprey

The MV-75 follows the same basic tiltrotor principle as the Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey, which has served with the US Marine Corps and Air Force for years.

However, the two aircraft use different designs. On the V-22, the engines and propellers tilt together, while the MV-75 keeps its engines fixed and tilts only the rotor assemblies. The newer aircraft is also being developed specifically for the Army’s long-range assault missions, rather than as a direct replacement for the Osprey.

From V-280 Valor to MV-75 Cheyenne II

The programme has its origins in the US Army’s Future Vertical Lift initiative, which was established to develop aircraft capable of replacing several existing helicopter types.

The Army launched the FLRAA competition in 2019, seeking an aircraft that could provide a substantial improvement in speed, range and operational flexibility.

Bell competed against a Sikorsky-Boeing team offering the Defiant X compound helicopter.

In December 2022, the Army selected Bell’s V-280-based design, awarding the company the contract to develop the future aircraft.

The decision represented one of the most significant changes in US Army aviation procurement in decades.

Rather than adopting another conventional helicopter, the Army chose a tiltrotor design intended to operate across much larger battlefields.

The MV-75 is not expected to replace every Black Hawk. Instead, it will take over part of the assault and utility mission while existing helicopters continue to serve in other roles.

The 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) has been identified as the first Army division scheduled to field the new aircraft.

The division specialises in moving troops by air and is expected to be among the first formations to develop operational tactics around the MV-75’s greater speed and range.

Why is it called Cheyenne II?

600The Army formally named the aircraft MV-75 Cheyenne II in April 2026, continuing its tradition of naming helicopters after Native American tribes.

The name honours the Northern Cheyenne Tribe in Montana and the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma.

The number 75 refers to 1775, the year the US Army was established.

The Cheyenne II designation also recalls the Lockheed AH-56 Cheyenne, an advanced attack helicopter developed for the Army during the 1960s.

That earlier programme was cancelled before the aircraft entered operational service.

“In naming the MV-75 Cheyenne II, we honour the enduring contributions of the Cheyenne people to our Nation – both their distinguished service in uniform and their legacy as steadfast protectors of their way of life,” said Colonel Jeffrey Poquette, the Army’s FLRAA project manager, when the name was announced.

“The name also reflects a connection to the bold vision of the AH-56 Cheyenne, while ‘II’ signifies a new era of innovation and capability.”

A different approach to Army aviation

Beyond its flight performance, the MV-75 is being designed with a modular electronic architecture intended to make future upgrades easier.

Bell says the MV-75’s open-system architecture will allow new equipment and capabilities to be integrated without extensive redesign of the aircraft.

The Army also expects the platform to undertake medical evacuation, tactical resupply and humanitarian assistance missions in addition to transporting assault troops.

Its ability to operate over longer distances could be particularly useful in regions where military units are dispersed across islands, remote terrain or areas with limited infrastructure.

]]> Chemical used to fight wildfires corroded US air tankers, NTSB reveals https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/chemical-fight-wildfires-corroded-us-air-tankers-ntsb-reveals/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:02:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57492 An NTSB investigation found extensive damage to two aircraft after they carried a newly approved fire retardant, exposing serious shortcomings in how firefighting chemicals are tested.

The post Chemical used to fight wildfires corroded US air tankers, NTSB reveals appeared first on AGN.

]]> A fire retardant approved by the US Forest Service caused extensive corrosion in two firefighting aircraft, damaging critical wing structures, engines and electrical systems during the 2023 wildfire season, a federal investigation has found.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the chemical, Fortress FR-200, had been cleared for use without adequate testing of its effects on aircraft structures. The findings have prompted two safety recommendations calling for tougher approval standards.

The investigation involved a BAe 146 operated by Neptune Aviation Services and an MD-87 operated by Aero Air. Both aircraft participated in a Forest Service trial of the magnesium chloride-based retardant.

The first indication of trouble came from maintenance inspections. What initially appeared to be deposits inside a retardant tank eventually led investigators to uncover damage extending well beyond the aircraft’s firefighting equipment.

A strange discovery inside the aircraft

On 16 July 2023, maintenance crews entered Neptune Aviation’s BAe 146 retardant tank after repeated problems with its liquid-level indication system. The aircraft had completed 64 drops of the new chemical.

Inside, technicians found black residue, hard crystalline deposits and a gelatinous substance resembling yoghurt. Much of the softer material washed away with water, but the crystals remained attached to components.

The problems persisted. By early August, after 107 drops, further deposits had accumulated around tank floats, switches and structural fasteners.

Aero Air’s MD-87 was showing different signs of deterioration. After just 20 loads of FR-200, inspectors found pitting on metal test samples inside its tank. In August, they discovered corrosion on two steel springs used to secure a tank ventilation door. One had fractured.

The full extent of the damage emerged during detailed inspections after the firefighting season.

On the MD-87, corrosion had affected primary wing structure, fuselage components, landing gear assemblies, electrical connectors, control cables and engines.

One structural component near the wing root had suffered corrosion extending through more than half its thickness in an affected area. Aero Air replaced the damaged section, along with more than 90 electrical connectors and several control cables.

Engine inspections revealed further problems. Technicians rejected 61 parts or modules from one engine and 53 from another because of excessive corrosion or contamination.

The speed of deterioration was particularly concerning. Aero Air reported that corrosion found on some flap components would ordinarily take 18 to 24 months to develop.

The MD-87 had entered tanker service less than three months earlier.

Investigators found no corresponding corrosion on comparable aircraft that had not carried FR-200.

Earlier warning signs

The investigation found that concerns about similar chemicals had emerged two years earlier.

During a 2021 evaluation, another Fortress product, FR-100, produced thick deposits when it came into contact with a conventional phosphate-based retardant.

The material became gel-like when wet and clay-like when dry. Operators reported problems with tank sensors, valves, flow meters and seals, alongside corrosion of hardware and deterioration of protective coatings.

The evaluation recommended additional testing of aircraft materials and further investigation of the chemical reactions.

Despite those findings, FR-200 received full Forest Service approval in December 2022.

Its operational evaluation had been conducted using a smaller, single-engine airtanker fitted with a fibreglass tank. That meant the tests did not adequately examine how the chemical would affect the combinations of metals and structural components found in larger aircraft.

The two large airtankers subsequently carried FR-200 during the first part of the 2023 season before alternating it with a conventional phosphate-based retardant.

The NTSB found that existing qualification procedures failed to assess the corrosion risks adequately, including those associated with mixing products based on different chemicals.

How the chemical gained approval

The Forest Service had revised its qualification requirements in 2020 to encourage competition and allow alternatives to traditional phosphate-based retardants.

Fortress subsequently introduced FR-100 and FR-200, the first new products added to the agency’s approved list in more than two decades.

However, the NTSB found that laboratory testing relied heavily on small, isolated metal samples rather than complete aircraft structures.

It did not adequately assess joints, fasteners, connected metals or the effects of repeated exposure to different chemicals.

The investigation also clarified that while the Federal Aviation Administration approves aircraft for aerial firefighting operations, the Forest Service decides which retardants may be carried and released.

Investigators demand tougher testing

The Forest Service suspended approval of FR-100 and FR-200 in May 2024 and removed both from its approved list that December.

It has since commissioned additional testing covering 20 aircraft materials and assemblies designed to better represent operating conditions.

However, the NTSB warned that these measures would not resolve the underlying problem unless the qualification rules themselves were changed.

The agency issued two recommendations calling for more realistic corrosion testing, developed with aircraft operators, manufacturers and technical specialists, and for those procedures to become mandatory when approving future retardants.

The concern extends beyond the cost of replacing damaged parts.

Corrosion can weaken an aircraft’s structure and, if undetected, eventually cause structural failure.

Google plans to use the data for product development and AI training.

The post Why is Google buying data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines? appeared first on AGN.

]]> A US bankruptcy judge has approved Google’s $10 million purchase of internal business records from Spirit Airlines. Google says it will use the material for product development and to train artificial intelligence models.

Judge Sean Lane approved the sale on 17 November, Reuters reported, after Google agreed to tighter safeguards for former employees’ data. The sale covers material from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as records relating to marketing, productivity and airline operations.

Spirit ceased flying on 2 May after talks over a government bailout collapsed. The ultra-low-cost carrier had returned to Chapter 11 in August 2025, hoping to recover through a reorganisation that included a substantial fleet reduction. 

The recovery was unsuccessful and, as Spirit wound down, its bankruptcy estate put the records up for auction. Google won the bidding in August with a $10 million offer. AI company Mercor was named the alternate bidder at $7.5 million, according to a bankruptcy court filing.

What does Google want with airline records?

Google’s plans for the records, reported by Reuters in August, are to use them as examples of how work moves between common business tools. The reporting did not identify which Google products or models would use the material.

An email can provide the context for a decision, a calendar can show when a team discussed it, and a spreadsheet can record the figures behind it. A dataset that keeps those connections intact can provide examples for training an AI model to bring together information scattered across different files, such as when answering a question about a project.

What happens to passenger and employee data?

The connections raised privacy concerns. As AGN reported in August, the flight attendants’ union challenged the proposed sale over the range of employee material potentially in scope. In its initial objection, the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA highlighted a provision in the original agreement that called for links between records to be preserved during de-identification. 

“Worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a whole new worker’s rights issue,” said Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA.

In an October letter, 121 US lawmakers warned that removing direct identifiers such as names and email addresses could still leave clues that allow information to be traced back to individuals.

Reuters reported that the consumer privacy ombudsman recommended approval in October after excluding personal information relating to 97 million Spirit customers from the transaction.

Under the revised terms, the flight attendants’ union said health and medical information, drug and alcohol testing records, disciplinary files, safety programme records and identification documents are excluded.

Data going to Google must undergo de-identification under the ISO/IEC 27559 international standard. An independent agent chosen in consultation with the unions will check the results. 

Google must handle the records in a secure environment and keep them confidential. The terms also bar Google from attempting to identify individuals in the dataset, the union said.

In a filing withdrawing objections on the day of the hearing, the union said the withdrawal would take effect once the court entered a written order substantially in the form negotiated with Spirit and Google.

]]> How Ukraine used 11 weapons systems to strike Russia’s Kerch Bridge https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ukraine-kerch-bridge-strike-11-drones-missiles/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57454 Ukrainian forces degraded Russian air defences in a seven-stage campaign, deploying Palianytsia, Flamingo, and Neptune weapons to collapse part of the Kerch Bridge.

The post How Ukraine used 11 weapons systems to strike Russia’s Kerch Bridge appeared first on AGN.

]]> Ukraine used 11 types of drones and missiles in a weeks-long operation against Russia‘s Kerch Bridge, culminating in strikes that brought down a major section of the road crossing and damaged the parallel railway linking Russia with Crimea.

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) and the military’s General Staff, involved attacks on Russian air defence systems, radars and electronic warfare equipment before the bridge itself was targeted on 16 and 17 November.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the final stage involved Palianytsia drones striking the road crossing, while Neptune missiles, Ruta drones and FP-5 weapons attacked the railway section.

The bridge’s road arch and the roadway beneath it collapsed into the Kerch Strait. Satellite imagery taken on 19 November showed approximately 225 metres of the road crossing had fallen into the water, with additional damage visible on the railway section.

The operation offers an unusually detailed account of how Ukraine combined domestically developed long-range weapons against a heavily defended target. It also shows how the country’s missile and drone programmes have expanded since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

Seven stages before the final strike

Zelensky described the attack as the seventh stage of an operation conducted over several weeks.

Ukrainian forces first targeted the equipment protecting the crossing, including surface-to-air missile systems, surveillance radars and electronic warfare installations.

Those systems perform different tasks. Radars detect and track approaching aircraft and missiles. Surface-to-air missiles attempt to intercept them, while electronic warfare equipment can interfere with satellite navigation and communications used by attacking drones.

Ukraine’s approach was to weaken those defences before launching the main attack.

The President identified Dovbush, Vendetta, Da Vinci, Sichen, MICH-2000, An-197, FP-1, Ruta, Palianytsia, FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptune as the weapons involved across the operation.

He did not disclose how many of each were launched.

The SBU said its Alpha special forces unit used Palianytsia weapons against the road section during the decisive attack. Russian authorities acknowledged structural damage and suspended traffic across the bridge.

“For years, the russians have been trying to convince the world that the Crimean bridge is one of the most heavily defended structures on the planet. Today, its remains lie on the seabed. It was not just the bridge that collapsed; the myth of russia’s greatness has once again been shaken. Through unique special operations, the Security Service is achieving the impossible and bringing a just peace closer to Ukraine,” the SSU said in a statement.

Flamingo brings a heavier warhead

Among the weapons named by Zelensky, the FP-5 Flamingo is particularly significant because of its size and payload.

Developed by Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point, Flamingo is a ground-launched cruise missile intended to attack fixed targets at long distances.

The company claims a range of up to 3,000km, a maximum speed of 950km/h and a payload of approximately 1,150–1,200kg. Those are manufacturer specifications, not independently verified figures for its performance during the bridge attack.

Flamingo is considerably larger than the one-way attack drones Ukraine has used extensively against Russian military and industrial targets.

According to an assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), its propulsion system appears to use an Ivchenko AI-25TL turbofan, a type originally developed for crewed aircraft.

The IISS assessment also described the missile as a large, subsonic weapon that does not incorporate the stealth characteristics of more sophisticated cruise missiles.

Its principal advantage is the ability to carry a much heavier explosive payload than smaller attack drones. That distinction matters when attacking substantial infrastructure rather than relatively exposed equipment or vehicles.

Zelensky said Ukrainian forces used Flamingo in a precision-guided strike and that its communications uplink remained operational until the final seconds.

He did not explain how the link was maintained or whether operators could change the missile’s aim during its final approach.

Palianytsia and Neptune attack separate crossings

Ukraine attributed the destruction of the road section to Palianytsia, a jet-powered, long-range attack weapon.

Palianytsia has been described as a drone-missile because it combines characteristics of an unmanned aircraft and a cruise missile. Unlike a conventional propeller-driven attack drone, it uses jet propulsion.

Ukrainian defence claims it has a range of up to 700 km, a speed of around 900km/h and carry a 100kg warhead.

The R-360 Neptune, meanwhile, began life as a Ukrainian anti-ship cruise missile.

It became widely known after Ukraine used Neptune missiles against the Russian Black Sea Fleet flagship Moskva in April 2022. The cruiser subsequently sank.

Ukraine has since developed land-attack versions of the Neptune family, allowing it to strike fixed targets ashore.

The variant used against the Kerch Bridge has not been identified publicly.

Neptune missiles were among the weapons directed at the railway crossing on 17 November. Ukraine’s military also reported a further Neptune attack overnight on 18–19 November, saying the railway tracks had been damaged.

Ruta and Ukraine’s drone arsenal

Ruta was another weapon used against the railway section.

Associated with European manufacturer Destinus, Ruta is a jet-powered strike system designed for longer-range attacks.

Published information describes two versions with different payloads and ranges. The Block 1 variant has a range of about 300km and a 150kg warhead, while Block 2 is credited with approximately 700km and a 250kg warhead.

It remains unclear which version Ukraine used.

The FP-1, developed by Fire Point, is a different type of weapon. It is a propeller-driven, fixed-wing one-way attack drone intended for long-distance missions.

Several other Ukrainian drones took part in the wider campaign.

Dovbush is a family of unmanned aircraft. The long-range T40 version may have been involved, although Ukraine has not confirmed the variant.

Sichen is reported to have a range of up to 1,400km and a payload of around 40kg. MICH-2000 is another long-range drone, with published figures indicating a range of up to 2,000km and a payload between 25kg and 60kg.

Da Vinci has been described as a strike drone capable of carrying approximately 25–40kg.

Much less is publicly established about Vendetta and An-197.

What was actually destroyed?

The Kerch Bridge consists of separate road and railway crossings extending approximately 19km between Russia’s Taman Peninsula and Crimea.

The November attacks caused the collapse of the road bridge’s main metal arch and a substantial section of roadway.

Satellite images published after the strikes confirmed the scale of that damage.

Why the crossing matters

Russia opened the road bridge in 2018, four years after annexing Crimea. The railway connection followed later.

The crossing has since served as an important transport route for passengers, freight and military supplies moving between Russia and the peninsula.

Ukraine previously attacked it in October 2022, July 2023 and June 2025, using methods that included a truck bomb, naval drones and underwater explosives.
